en: Preface to the *Xianguo suilu* (Record Following Present Results):
Now, cause and effect are like a form and its shadow. Once the form exists, the shadow necessarily follows.
If one wishes to rectify the shadow, one must first straighten the form. If the form is straightened, how could the shadow not be rectified? Yet, if one does not straighten the form...
If one desires its reflection to be upright, it is like stirring boiling soup while failing to stop the fire; though one may wish for it to cool, such a thing is impossible.
This is the universal teaching of our Dharma-gate. It is also found in the secular classics, where we speak of "hidden virtue" (*yīn dé*) and "manifest retribution" (*yáng bào*).
Is this not precisely what I have taught regarding cause and effect? There are those in the world who do not believe in cause and effect; their ignorance is profound.
It is even more so; let us set it aside for now and not discuss it further. This year, in the year Wuyin (1698), while I was residing at Huangbo, Mr.
Rintō happened to bring a transcribed copy of a work and visit me, saying: "This is the *Xianguo suilu* (Record of Manifest Karmic Results).

May I propose carving it into woodblocks to circulate it throughout the world? Is this permissible or not? I took it up and read it, whereupon I learned that it was the notes of Bawang Jixian of Lingyin Monastery. Jixian—

Master Shijude was a disciple of Venerable Heshang. Since Heshang was one of my own followers under Tiantong, his words regarding the matter of my record of the relics of Master Fei at Jingshan may be taken as authoritative testimony.
Furthermore, reading his treatises which highly extol the merit of reciting the Buddha’s name, it is clear that he was a member of the Lotus Society.
This entire compilation records only those matters I have personally heard or witnessed through my current experience.
Regarding "experiencing manifest results": other instances such as past causes with subsequent retribution (*paścātpāka*) or maturation (*vipāka*) are not what is intended here.
I say that the venerable elder’s single-minded compassion has, without his realizing it, dragged him through the mud and water. For those of noble resolve, both within and beyond the world—
Do not disregard these words because they appear shallow or mundane. They are not only a blessing for this retired elder, but also a blessing for all readers.
This compilation may be read alongside such works as the *Zizhi* (Self-Knowledge) and the *Yinzhi* (Secret Blessings).
What is there to prevent Mr. Tō from carving and publishing it? — Jieshi Jingshou.
Table of Contents for the *Xianguo Suilu* (Records of Manifested Retribution),
Volume One.
Bestowed with Vision by the Great Being of the Pass Temple through the Protective Power of Chen Yixiu.
Zhao Zhiqing retired from office to practice cultivation, foreseeing and thus avoiding disaster;
Zhao Shiyong gave a single coin to an extraordinary monk and subsequently obtained a filial heir;
Xu Chengmin personally administered the underworld offices and published the judgments of the netherworld.
When Master Yuantong received the full precepts, he was suddenly liberated from impermanence.
Zhu Gang’s soul traveled to the underworld, where his past lives were adjudicated;
Master Yinyuan used ritual repentance and the offering of food to dissolve these long-standing grudges.
Bi Fan’s destruction of the Tathāgata’s robe and bowl caused his arm to instantly shrink;
Zhang Bin rescued his master from peril by means of *nianfo* coins;
and Wu Jiao’s dedication of merit through *nianfo* while pouring oil over a candle led him to pass away at a predetermined time.
Wu Shubo received the precepts and recited the Buddha’s name at the moment of death, whereupon a lotus flower emerged from the earth;
Wang Jian was mistakenly summoned back to life and personally recounted his experiences in the netherworld;
and Mr. Zhou, by refusing illicit wealth in secret, immediately attained the highest rank in the imperial examinations.
The former Prefect Gu was drowned for his total devotion to principle, a consequence made manifest by his prior deeds;
the current Intendant Zhang encountered peril for upholding integrity, yet divine protection preserved his integrity;
Wei Yingzhi later recalled his vow of fasting and ultimately brought about his own death by hanging.
The Layman Wang Qi lost mindfulness and sold his vegetarian provisions, which immediately brought about his death;
the tutelary deity, loathing such defilement and sacrilege, manifested its numinous power to drag him from the temple.
Scroll Two.
Wu Zhanlou’s cultivation was recorded in the registers and auspicious signs appeared in the Western Quarter;
Master Ruowan mistakenly stepped on a stone, which led a mad monk to deliver a message;
the Shi family’s pig was spared from slaughter after receiving a dream, whereupon it threw itself into a Chan temple.
Traveling under the stars, he returned home and recited incantations from memory, thereby escaping the boiling oil;
a monk in Wuchang was spared from being harmed by a pig; at Jiangxin, he summoned a karmic retribution;
Wang Zifang donated the rafters and beams of Zhaokong Temple, greatly manifesting spiritual wonders.
When Magistrate Wang carved the *Jinjing* (Golden Sutra) from the fish-head [carving] for circulation in the world,
Zhao Chao-feng returned with a *Luohan* belt and consequently built a great temple;
when Imperial Censor Wang constructed the Ancestral Hall of Medicine, he obtained a son and was spared from calamity.
Weng Zhang repaid a kindness by returning gold, whereby his descendants flourished for generations;
Qian Zhouhou invited a Vinaya master to receive the precepts, whereupon a Buddha image appeared in the candle flame;
Ge Langyu and his son carved a "Book of Exhortation to Goodness" and distributed it to others, through which their entire family was spared from calamity.
Sun Xuexian erected a stele for the restoration of the Arhat statue at Beifeng Peak;
he solicited stone pillars from the Five Saints (Wusheng) to assist in the construction of the Great Hall at Lingyin Monastery;
and during a Water and Land ceremony in Taicang, spirits and ghosts manifested supernatural wonders.
Record of Extraordinary Events During the Kṣitigarbha Repentance Retreat at Anchan Hermitage in Kunshan:
Zhang Erqiu was moved by a dream after eating meat;
Gong Ermou’s exhortation to cultivate goodness through extensive giving led to the descent of a deity and the manifestation of spiritual efficacy upon the completion of the retreat.
The two Heavenly Kings manifested miraculous wonders at the main hall of Shushan Monastery;
Li Qianbu obtained a son through the creation of an image and maintained his integrity from beginning to end;
and although Li Bokxin harbored thoughts of murder, he was instead killed by a "heart-demon."
The old man who had long been ill rejoiced at the repayment of his former debts, and his mind was suddenly cleared of the "snake and horse" [distractions].
Because the Censor suffered misfortune, he abandoned his vegetarian fast and eventually returned to the Way of the Spirits.
Volume Three.
Qian Bo-yun, having studied Buddhism in his old age, ultimately attained the Western Paradise;
Huang She-liu was resolute in his devotion to the West and passed away at a predetermined time;
and Wang Feng-chang, whose family had accumulated merit over generations and enjoyed a continuous succession of imperial degrees, [attained liberation].
Tan Xianqing established a Great Compassion Altar to pray for progeny and was first granted two sons;
because his lordship served the Buddha with such refined piety, he repeatedly received miraculous responses.
At Upper Tianzhu, he cast a bronze statue of the Bodhisattva, which manifested its spiritual power by personally bestowing yellow clay upon him.
The Manifestation of Miraculous Treasures and Traces by the Frog Messenger of Jinxian County;
the Descent of the Pen by Zhang Zhenjun of Anguo Temple in Huangzhou through a Minor Servant;
and Xu Yishi’s Sacrifice of Wealth to Benefit the People, whereby he Swiftly Attained a Noble Reward.
Yu Chunjiao avoided the calamity of fire by providing meals for monks, thereby increasing his meritorious practice;
Master Zhu was able to remain whole during a fire disaster because he had prepared ritual methods in advance with the monks;
and Jiang Sugu passed the examination for the recommendation of worthy scholars because he continued the lineage of the Bodhisattva’s instructions.
Yin Xuānzǐ performed repentance rites for a perilous situation and was ultimately saved;
Zhāng Zhěntái received a vision of Wéitiān in a dream and the state was restored.
Thus, the two men experienced different retributions—honor and disgrace—based on their respective reverence and negligence toward Guāndì.
Zhang Qiguang disobeyed his dreams and, through his greed for eating turtle meat, met his death;
Wang Zhishi, because of his evil nature, was reborn as a snake as a residual retribution for his past life;
and the butcher of Hankou, refusing the monk’s advice, immediately incurred a cruel retribution.
The pig of Gaoyou sacrificed its body to repay the matting it had consumed throughout its life;
the butcher household of Penglang Town immediately reaped the karmic retribution for slaughtering cattle;
and the Daoist priest who greedily devoured temple property turned his next life into that of a donkey.
Cao Han, who had massacred a city, encountered the conditions for salvation like a pig;
the grievous injustice of Monk Cong of Wujiang Road was fully vindicated;
and when Magistrate Wang was appointed to the region of Wu, he cleared the wrongs of the frogs.
Wang Xiajiang declined official office to practice the Way, whereupon he suddenly attained the fruits of the Path;
a merchant, through sincere devotion, made offerings to the Buddha and spared a captive from slaughter;
a man struck a bronze Buddha image with a hammer yet it remained unharmed, and the calamity instead befell his seller.
The Paralyzed Man Cured by Prostrating to Avalokiteśvara;
Establishing Conditions through the Devotion of a Huizhou Merchant Who Resolutely Offered Incense and Was Saved from the Peril of Fire.
Scroll Four.
In Huangzhou, flying fires raged and burned everything except the monk’s quarters;
a poor woman donated a single coin to cast a Buddha, and her virtuous deed remains undiminished.
At Mount Yao, a monk stole the oil for the Vemacitra deity lamp and was immediately visited by divine retribution.
The ghost of Vairocana’s tower summoned two scholars to collect a debt; once the payment was made, they revived.
Two scholars treated Wenchang with contempt; their physical records were both destroyed.
Two scholars inherited arrogance toward Dizang; they died immediately and received retribution.
A commoner of Jianchang defiled the Three Jewels and was struck dead by the Thunder God;
a person of Yongcheng suffered a sudden calamity for defiling a pagoda or temple;
Chen Xiang slaughtered dogs and relied on his evil without remorse, yet manifested retribution in this very life.
Xiong Ji-na protected the Dharma with such devotion that he obtained an heir within the appointed time;
Gu the Scholar was transformed into a crane and returned to life, whereupon his search confirmed the truth;
and Huang Feng-weng moved the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara) through his practice of goodness so that the Bodhisattva sent him a son, thereby establishing a great name and integrity.
Wu Xiashou burned his body to the death for the sake of loyalty, and his spirit ascended to heaven;
Shi Feng’eng performed long-term vegetarian rites for monks and was moved by his son’s attainment of the highest imperial examination;
Yang Jun saved a man at the crossroads and thereby brought warmth and prosperity to his household.
Master Wu encountered a celestial immortal yet, out of attachment to life, he squandered a rare karmic connection;
the blind man, with a malicious heart, attempted to rob and kill him, thereby instantly forfeiting his own life.
Conversely, Lady Wu Dao’ao, through her devout recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, passed away in a seated posture, manifesting wondrous signs.
The Fang family, through sincere devotion and ritual recitation, had their entire household returned alive;
Xu Ziwei, by examining characters from his previous life, attained a high rank in the imperial examinations;
and Dong Qi, who had taken advantage of others with false scales, saw his family fortune secretly depleted.
After the passing of the Old Monk Feiyin, his body was cremated and many śarīras were manifested;
Chan Master Yuanzhi of Caoxi attained realization through diligent cultivation and manifested auspicious signs at the end;
and the Venerable Tianbai, who concluded his life by reciting the Lotus Sūtra, heard celestial music at his death.
Xin Jie was spared from the registers of the hells because he had previously performed acts of goodness, even though his tally of merit was incomplete;
Wei Tian was reborn as a servant to a king because he had shown such a response [to his past].
Yunchou suffered the retribution of becoming a snake because of his evil nature and his beating of his wife.
The son of the Cai family was restored to life through the manifest response of the Lingyin Monastery deity;
a monk from Jiangbei, who was attached to his remaining wealth, attained liberation through the performance of memorial rites;
and Wang Yangquan attained rebirth in the Pure Land by reforming his occupation and practicing cultivation.
A fisherman who used a clever ruse to drown someone was immediately executed as retribution;
Li Wenxue suffered intense agony for smearing ink on the *Platform Sutra*;
and Zhi Xiyou’s official rank and records were instantly extinguished for accidentally causing the loss of human life.
Record of Manifest Karmic Results, Volume One (All instances of present causes and effects that were personally seen or heard are included in this record).
Recorded by Jie Xian, the Retired Elder Heishan Qiao of Lingyin Monastery.
Chen Yixiu, who used his strength to protect the Guanyin Temple, was granted eyesight as a reward.
Chen Yixiu, courtesy name Yusi, was a native of Jinning Prefecture in Shandong.

While he was still a common scholar (*zhusheng*), he observed that Yang Shenghua and others of the Muslim faith intended to demolish the Temple of Lord Guan and expand the local Muslim mosque. Mr. Chen petitioned the authorities with great effort, and the matter was suppressed.
Later, in the spring of the Guiwei year, when rebel bandits breached Guanzhou, Yang Shenghua and his followers gathered several hundred or a thousand men.
The Zhòngchéngbiàn militia encountered Cáo Gōng on their way back with the Huihuī troops.
Driven by former resentment, they called out to the crowd, beat him to death instantly, gouged out both his eyes, and further blinded them with ash. They then cast his corpse into his own house.

Cáo Gōng himself perceived that he had transformed into a *antarābhava* (intermediate state) body, only about two chi in height, remaining within his corpse. One night, he suddenly saw Guānshèng descend.
His family said to him, "Our lot does not include this temple either; it is simply difficult for us to grant you such kindness at the cost of our own lives.
However, your allotted lifespan has not yet ended, and you surely have a share of fame and office.

We shall cause you to return to life. Chen replied, "I am grateful for the great kindness of the Great Sage. Yet, my two eyes have already been lost; even if I return to the world of the living, I am already [blind]."
"A blind man—how could he possibly resume reading books or pursue the career of an examination candidate? Guansheng also reflected for a moment and then said, "It shall be no hindrance.
I shall request the Great Being Avalokiteśvara to come; He will surely grant you back your sight. Having spoken, he immediately ascended into the air and departed.
A short while later, he returned and said, "The Great Being has arrived. Soon, they saw the Great Being, his body draped in white robes.
He appeared like an immortal lady, fully endowed with all the marks of excellence. Lord Guan pointed to Mr. Chen and requested on his behalf that he be granted eyes.
The Bodhisattva smiled and said, "This is not difficult at all. He then called out once into the air;
suddenly, a celestial youth appeared, carrying a large wicker basket covered with lotus leaves. When the Bodhisattva lifted the covering, they were all eyes. Immediately—
The Bodhisattva took two pills in his hand and had Chen take a cup of wine to swallow them. Chen drank it against his will;
there was a gurgling sound, and he suddenly awoke. His intermediate state (antarābhava) form immediately vanished, and Chen’s eyes were restored within both sockets.
After the Great Being had departed, the Holy One of Guan sent him off and said to Chen: "You need not think further of seeking revenge. Before long, the Great Qing..."

"Once these people arrive, not a single soul shall remain. Next year, you shall achieve successive successes in the examinations. Indeed, in the year of Yiyou (1625), he passed the provincial examination. Suddenly, a person sent him a letter containing the following verses:

(Chen) "On the eastern side, ears are just beginning to grow. (Yi) "At the head of the grass, eight bloods are complete. (Xiu) "One night, three people lie down. (Guan) "Within the gate, eight heavens are hidden. (Gong) "The old man has attained transcendence.

(Mo) "A black dog [is there]. (You) "The person on the right leads it. (Lian) "Beside the ear. [Note: These are word puzzles based on the characters for the names Chen, Yi, Xiu, Guan, Gong, Mo, You, and Lian.]

Silken threads fall in disarray. (A stage direction: *kezi*) The characters "禾" (*he*) and "斗" (*dou*) are forever linked. Chen Yixiu did not understand the significance of this; he hurriedly looked for the person [who had spoken it], but they had already vanished.
On the back of the document, nine large characters were inscribed: "Chen Yixiu, Guāngōng's silent protection, linked in the examination. Only then did he realize its meaning.

He indeed passed the jinshi examination in the Bingxu year and served as a Langzhong in the Ministry of Revenue. He was subsequently appointed as the Acting Governor of Jingzhou. Later, flowers bloomed [as a sign]. [Composition by] Hou Shenghua.
"During the rebellion, thirteen members of his clan were executed by slicing at the marketplace.
My elder brother Ba-ung said: 'I first heard of this matter from Master Chen Minzhao, who recorded it in the *Collected Works of King Wuchan* for my disciple Gu Yiren.
Furthermore, Xu Changwu, the Magistrate of Huangmei, also said this."
I am his relative by marriage. His story is most certain; there is no one who has not seen it with their own eyes.

However, his eyes were slightly small, and when he gazed straight ahead, light would overflow from them, differing somewhat from ordinary people. Alas! Lord Chen, out of a virtuous heart, protected the temple and was moved by this extraordinary circumstance.
Through this, the Great Being used his thousand hands and eyes to turn blindness into sight once more—truly vast is his supernormal power.
The mouth of the sea is difficult to describe. The retributions of the spirits and Buddhas are swifter than turning over one’s palm. How can one not stand in awe?
Zhao Zhiqing, who hung up his official cap to practice the Way, avoided disaster through foresight.
Zhao Zhiqing was a native of Shandong. Selected as a filial and incorrupt official (xiaolian), he served as the Magistrate of Zanghuang County in Hejian Prefecture. Having held office for three...
He was upright, intelligent, benevolent, and compassionate; the myriad people praised his virtue. One day, he went to the residence of Governor Ling Shenggong to request his resignation.
When the Governor asked why, Zhao replied, "Because I have come to know the causes and conditions of my past lives, I cannot help but return home."
The Great Governor became even more astonished by this and asked about his past lives. Zhao replied, "In a previous existence, I was a student of the sutras under a certain Great Dharma Master.
That Dharma Master possessed the power of meditative concentration (samādhi) and the ability to penetrate wisdom.

When I was twenty-six years old and my illness reached its critical point, the Master said to me: 'Your power of the Way (mārga-bala) is not yet firm; you have already entered the realm of red merit (puṇya). "

"I have never cultivated great merit, nor could I ever ascend the official examination rankings; I am merely a filial and incorruptible district magistrate. However, my term is limited to three years.

If even one day exceeds that, great calamity will immediately arrive. You should withdraw with courage from the turbulent current, enter the mountains to practice cultivation, and you shall still be able to see me.
Having finished speaking, he passed away. From the moment he entered and left the mother's womb, his original nature was never deluded; it remained vividly clear.
All these were proven true. Now that the three-year term has expired, he has resolved to enter the mountains.

He urged the Prefect to petition the High Commissioner (Zhizhi Gong) so that Li Guankui could be allowed to return home before being replaced; however, shortly thereafter, a man surnamed Liu was appointed to fill his vacancy.
Less than half a month later, bandits arrived and utterly destroyed the city; the entire family was killed.
The retired elder said: "Ling Shengong, whose courtesy name is Bizheng, was a fellow villager and member of the same literary society as I.

Initially selected as an envoy (xingren), he was appointed as the Prefect of Jianchang, then transferred to the Prefecture of Hejian. Upon returning home after completing his term, he recounted this matter to me."
Li Guankxi, whose taboo name was Mo and courtesy name Zimu, observed the long fast and studied Buddhism; he too was my fellow practitioner of the Way. His words were no different from mine.
Zhao Shiyong gave a single coin to an extraordinary monk and immediately obtained a worthy son.
Liu of Xibian, Macheng, accompanied his paternal cousin Liu Shen to Gucheng County in Zhending Prefecture to serve as a presiding examiner.
He had once secretly saved the lives of two men. Later, when the rebel troops of Chang arrived and the city fell, the county magistrate fled to seek refuge.
Mr. Liu escorted the magistrate’s family back toward Huangtu, where he was encountered by rebel soldiers and killed. His spirit returned to Macheng to visit [the deceased].

At Mount Dong, the Emperor said, "Since you have saved two lives, you shall surely attain a favorable rebirth. The Emperor ordered his attendants to search among the virtuous families within the city for those who were childless.
The officials reported to the Emperor that there was a physician named Zhao Fengyi, styled Shiyong. The Emperor ordered them to consult the registers of good and evil deeds to examine his case.
They saw that Master Zhao had once drowned five daughters; by law, he ought to be cut off from progeny. They then checked the register of the virtuous.
[The Emperor] saw that in a certain year, amidst a great snowfall, he had once given one coin to a cold-begging monk.
The monk was actually a Bodhisattva who had assumed the appearance of a beggar to test him. The Emperor said, "The merit of this single coin is very great; it should be granted to his successor.

He then dispatched Liu Jun to take rebirth. As he was about to depart, the Emperor said to him, "When you have been away for nine years, there shall be a filial and incorruptible official (xiaolian)."
I present this to your wife. In such-and-such a year you entered the local academy; in such-and-such a year you were granted a stipend. Throughout your life, you shall enjoy abundant blessings.
Later, Zhao gave birth to a son who, as soon as he emerged from the womb, cried out, "I am Liu [Name] of Xiban!
The Emperor of the Eastern Peak has sent me to be the successor to Zhao; there is no need for further words. However, during my lifetime, I still had property and loans outstanding. He—
This was not yet clear. [The Emperor] quickly summoned my wife and children. Zhao Shi-yong immediately invited his wife to bring them there.

The boy enumerated their old debts one by one, ordering his wife and children to collect according to the promissory notes; there was not even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy. At nine years of age, he indeed became the son-in-law of the Licentiate Deng.
Subsequently, his career in officialdom and his life’s path were exactly as the Emperor had ordained.
The Retired Elder said: "Regarding this matter, my friend Mei Huilian has a record of it in circulation.
In the winter of the Wuxu year, while I was at Anguo Temple in Huangzhou, I suffered from a severe and painful spleen ailment.
It happened that Zhang Longyu, the Provincial Commander-in-Chief, invited Master Zhao Shiyong to his office to attend to my illness; he cured me at once. I then asked about the birth of his son."
Dì asked, "Is what you have said truly authentic? Zhaojun replied, "It is a thousandfold truth, a myriadfold truth. I then inquired after his given name and style name.
Zhao said, "It is precisely for this reason that my name is Mo (Silence) and my style name is Ruoyuyan (Weak Speech).
Furthermore, all the various legal cases from the underworld of Mount Tai were recounted by my son."
Xu Chengmin, who served in the Office of the Netherworld, published the *Mingpan Taicang* (The Netherworld Judgments of Taicang Xu Chengmin).
He was the son of Xiusheng of the local academy; from his youth, he maintained the fasts and delighted in goodness, forming a society with friends to recite the Buddha’s name.
Suddenly, he received an imperial decree to serve as an official in the netherworld. Beginning from the Gengwu year of the Chongzhen era, he was a scholar by day.
At night, he adjudicated matters of the underworld. Every day at the hour of midnight, he would sit in the central hall in darkness;

his body and breath were both cold, and his two eyes stared upward. He summoned the ghosts of both parties and rendered judgments as fluidly as flowing water, his voice resonant and stern while a chilling wind blew around him.
To his left and right, lamps, paper, and pens were placed for recording; these were compiled into a large volume titled *Loudong Mingpan* (Judgments from the Underworld of Loudu).
It circulated everywhere throughout the Nine Provinces. Its judgment of good and evil and its retribution for deeds were like looking into a mirror or gazing upon a high terrace;

those who read it were struck with awe, their hair standing on end even without cold. The Retired Official said, "This was a friend from my Gengwu-year Buddha-recitation assembly. He was a man of pure, honest, and simple character, as straightforward as wood."
He was taciturn; apart from reading books, he knew nothing other than reciting the Buddha’s name. Suddenly, he received an appointment as a celestial official.
His voice was resonant and clear, and every word and phrase was as decisive as driving a nail through iron—this was already extraordinary. Yet even more marvelous was this:

he had never set eyes upon the scriptures of the Three Teachings, yet whenever he faced legal interrogation, he would cite the classics and historical records, drawing freely from the Buddhist canon, word for word.
It is exquisitely carved; truly, it is inexplicable. Among the dark judgments (*mingpan*), there are several public cases (*gongan*) that emerged from my own records.
I have not added a single punctuation mark, nor have I ever increased or decreased a single character. This has continued for over ten years. Cheng Min then composed his own testimony:
"At first, I was an assistant magistrate for Lord Yan. After death, I truly received this office. This is a case from former years in Lou East.
A truly extraordinary matter! This is something witnessed with my own eyes and experienced by my very body.
Master Yuantong had received the full precepts and was suddenly liberated from impermanence.
Master Yuantong was a native of Meili in Changshu. Having observed the fasts since middle age, he was suddenly summoned by a decree from Lord Yan.
When those who have gathered their lives first arrive at the Netherworld, they see outside the main gate a well-pavilion. An official bearing a talisman arrives;

he wears a leather tunic, carries a large apron, and wears a tiger mask. Upon looking into the well once, his body immediately soars into the air. Crossing seas and piercing mountains, he travels thousands of miles in an instant.
Those whom he has gathered are bound with wooden staffs and carried upon his shoulders as he flies through the air, even if there are only one or two.
The ten men were as light as feathers. They took turns on duty every five days. Yuantong grew weary of this and sought a way out by every means, but was unable to escape.

He then left home to shave his head and become a monk. Continuing his duties as before, he eventually arrived at Xuanmu in the winter of the Yiyou year, where he went before the Venerable Master Poshuo to receive the Great Ordination of the Three Platforms.
When the precepts were completed, his labor was immediately abolished, and he would never again be conscripted as a "soul-summoning messenger.
The Abbot Ba'an said: "Master Hui was my closest friend; he was also a native of Meili and was a most intimate and close associate of Master Yuan.
Seeing that he had served for over ten years before being released, it is clear that this is what the Tathāgata ordained."
That the pure and great precepts are thus esteemed within the netherworld is truly extraordinary!
Zhu Gang’s "Discourse on Roaming the Netherworld and Judging Affairs in Previous Lives," by an elderly Confucian of Jiaxing named Zhu Gang:
Throughout his life, he was upright and scrupulous; he held considerable faith in Buddhism and Daoism. Suddenly one day—
One day, he saw two messengers from the underworld arrive to summon him. He followed them forward until they reached a great palace, which he knew to be the realm of the dead.
After a short while, Lord Yan struck the drum and ascended the throne. The gatekeeper announced, "The Prefect of Dongchang Prefecture enters."
Upon hearing this, Lord Zhu was no longer startled. As he ascended the steps, Lord Yan descended from his seat to exchange greetings.
Once the guest and host were seated, Lord Yan said, "When you served in office, you adjudicated the case of the matricide at Xuchang; was that not perhaps excessive?
At these words, Lord Zhu suddenly saw the events of his previous life appear before him. He replied, "In Xuchang, it was indeed..."
He has never committed matricide; it was his wicked wife who poisoned his mother.

Upon returning from Xuchang, as soon as he learns of her condition, he ought to dismiss his wife and report her crime to the authorities to receive due punishment—only then would he be a filial son. Yet, because the bonds of affection are difficult to sever, he remains vague and patient with her, sharing even the same bedding.
Although he did not personally kill his mother, according to the *Chunqiu*, this is equivalent to the case of Prince Xu.

Regarding the case of Zhao Dun, who tasted the medicine [of his mother] without crossing the border, the judgment was passed against him. This is one who participated in the extreme act of murdering his own mother.
To judge that he "murdered his mother"—who would say it was not appropriate? Lord Yan nodded in agreement, saying, "Your words are most correct.

He then bowed and ordered [Zhao] down the steps, commanding that he be led through to tour the Underworld before being sent back to the realm of the living. From this point on, Master Zhu maintained a lifelong fast and devoted himself to spiritual cultivation. Du...
He had severed all ties with worldly affairs.
The retired elder said, "I once saw his son compile a veritable record of his father's life and distribute it widely among both monastics and laypeople, requesting me to write a preface;
thus, I know the details."
Master Yin-yuan performed a ritual of repentance and the releasing of food to dissolve long-standing grudges.

A monk from north of the river named Yin-yuan was studying at Tian-ning Monastery when he suddenly died in the sixth month of a certain year. His mother was in Tai-zhou, and when the news arrived, his skin was already adhering to his mat.
As they were about to prepare him for burial, he revived and spoke in detail of his previous life, having once served as a magistrate in a certain county. From... [text continues]

He embezzled silver from the treasury and cast the blame upon the treasurer, further plotting to kill him to silence him. The treasurer, driven to the utmost resentment, brought the matter before Lord Yan.
When the treasurer was summoned for interrogation, the Lord of the Netherworld advised him, saying, "Since he has left the household life to become a monk, why do you resolve to seek revenge?
Would it not be better to use the power of the Dharma to perform a rite of salvation for him? Having received this instruction, Yinyuan established a vow to practice for three years.

[He] performed the repentance ritual for the Thousand Buddhas by day; at night, he released [birds] at Mount Meng to release his long-standing resentment. The official nodded in agreement, and he was subsequently granted a return to life.
He then requested a messenger of the underworld to lead him on a tour of the netherworld. They arrived at a great assembly hall with a sign that read "Scripture-Replenishment Hall.
Within it were several hundred monks and Daoists chanting scriptures while riding upon light. In an instant, it grew dark again. Yinyuan asked where they were. The messenger of the underworld...
The messenger said, "This is a monk from the secular world who took charge of the donors' collection of the *Tripiṭaka*. Although he acquired wealth, he did not recite the scriptures;
therefore, he is here to make up for that. He was asked again, "Why does it become dark so suddenly? He replied, "It is because his karmic power is profound and heavy."
He was not permitted to complete the repairs; thus, the light appeared only after a long delay. As soon as it appeared, it was withdrawn, causing him to remain for a long time in the black prison.
Only when the hidden fullness returned to life did he fulfill his vow over three years, thereafter returning to study at Lingyin Monastery.
The Retired Elder said, "The monastics of Tianning and Lingyin have repeatedly told me that their circumstances are exactly the same. Regarding the matter of the missing sutra:
in this world, followers of both Buddhism and Daoism treat cause and effect as a child’s play; who knows that within the unseen realm (*adṛṣṭa*), not a single detail fails to correspond?
Rather than remaining long in the dark hells without the ability to recover the sutra, why not take advantage of this [opportunity]?"
To serve as a donor beneath the light of the sun, moon, and the three luminaries—how joyful is this merit!
If you delay even for a moment, what will it avail to bite your own navel?
Bi-fan destroyed the Tathāgata’s robes and alms bowl, causing them to shrink by one cubit.
There was once a wealthy monk named Bifan in Macheng who had donated a hundred pieces of gold to help the villagers build a defensive wall to protect the region.
His disciple Wufeng wished to receive the precepts, but Bifan did not permit it. The disciple fled at night to the abbot of Xingyan to receive the precepts and returned.
Upon seeing him, Bifan was filled with great rage; he tore his three robes to shreds, smashed his ceramic bowl, and only then went to sleep that night.
He immediately saw the Honored Deity Weituo in a state of violent rage, scolding him bitterly, saying, "Who are you that dares to destroy the Dharma-vessel of the Tathāgata?
He was about to strike him with his precious mace when Daofan knelt and begged for forgiveness.

The Deity Weituo said, "Considering that you have meritorious service in maintaining the monastery, I shall merely remove one arm. With the mace, he lightly tapped Daofan’s right arm once. Daofan let out a frantic cry.
He awoke. Within several days, his right arm suddenly shrank away until it was only seven or eight *cun* long; his fist was like a small tangerine hanging from his shoulder.
To this day, both master and disciple remain there.
The retired elder said: "My teacher’s nephew, Houmu, lived as a neighbor with Yuan and recounted the matter in great detail.
Zhang Bin was a humble commoner of Ningbo who saved his master from peril by means of *nianfo* coins.
He resided in the corridor of Minister Cui and made his living weaving straw sandals; he was by nature fond of cultivation."
He practiced the long fast and recited the Buddha’s name. At night, he would cut the grass fibers from his *púxié* sandals; for every single bead of the rosary he recited, he would mark one fiber.
He collected these in a bamboo basket and, every year on New Year’s Eve, burned them inside the treasury of the Guanyin Hall at Dizang Monastery.

This has continued for nearly ten years. Recently, Minister Cui suffered from carbuncles and died; upon arriving in the underworld, the Lord of the Netherworld glared at him and began to recount his past deeds.
The day passed in evil. Duke Cui said, "Can you allow me to return to the world of the living so that I may cultivate meritorious deeds to atone for my sins?
The Lord of the Netherworld replied, "All that you have accumulated is 'karmic currency,' which is of no use here. As for your tenant, Zhang Bin—"

"Conversely, there are several storehouses of gold and silver here that can be exchanged for ten thousand [coins]. If you bring these, your offense may be absolved. Cui said, "I will simply release me so that I may return;
this matter is extremely easy. Zhang Bin replied, "I am utterly destitute; how could I provide such wealth?

The Lord of the Netherworld said, "For every person who observes the fasts and precepts with a sincere heart and recites the Buddha’s name once, one coin is deposited here. Or, if they recite it while their mind is distracted..."
For every utterance of the Buddha’s name by the Buddha, he also dropped one silver coin. Zhang Bin recited the Buddha’s name with a sincere heart, using the tassels of his rush shoes to keep count;
they accumulated until there were several *cang* (measures) of them. He then released Cui Huiyang and immediately called out to Zhang Bin, saying:

"In the underworld, you have accumulated a great deal of gold and money; you may exchange ten thousand of it and give it to me. Zhang Bin insisted that he had none. Cui Gong said: "You used your rush..."
It was the practice of counting the laces of one’s shoes; this refers to those who burn paper for Kṣitigarbha in an incense burner.

Zhang Bin said, "This is indeed true. If it truly has efficacy, then let it be as you wish. He then had a contract written and exchanged it for ten thousand pieces of real silver, requesting a monk to burn the contract and dedicate the merit.
Cui’s illness gradually improved. Zhang Bin said, "I am already advanced in years; I have no further use for these things."
He then used that silver to construct a large bridge at a cost of several thousand *qian*. He further built a hermitage to accommodate the assembly, which is still known today as Zhangbin.
Ba’eng said: "In the past, when I was lodging in the official residence of the Prefect Qian Xisheng, his elder and younger brothers several times..."
I am speaking of this matter. In the year Dingchou, I visited the Venerable Elder Mi of Tiantong; he too once crossed this bridge. This is certainly factual and not erroneous.
Because Zhang Bin recited the Buddha’s name with a sincere heart, his wealth accumulated until it filled his storehouses.
Later, he further used these funds to build bridges and welcome the assembly. If such vast merit and virtue can be dedicated toward rebirth in the Western Pure Land, [it will surely be attained].
He has certainly ascended high and shall never fall back. Such is the extraordinary excellence of the benefits of *nien-fo*. Alas, that the realms of the unseen and the seen are separated;
the people of this world do not know [of these benefits]. How can we raise Zhang Bin from the dead to proclaim this everywhere to both monastics and laypeople?
Wu Jiaoche, who made merit through the practice of nianfo, passed away at his appointed time;
he was a minor commoner from Suzhou surnamed Wu. He earned his livelihood by making candles, and thus his name became known for that craft. He rented a single room in Loumen.

Jie observed the fast with lifelong dedication. Day and night he recited the Buddha’s name, believing that because his sincerity was so profound, the owners of the ten or so large candle shops inside and outside Wuchang vied with one another to welcome him.
He regarded the pouring of oil upon the candles as an act of making offerings to the Three Jewels, the divine objects of refuge;

thus, he would invariably recite the Buddha’s name several times before pouring a single ladle of oil. He continued in this manner throughout his life until he reached over seventy years of age. Suddenly, he spoke to a close relative:
The shopkeeper said, "I have accumulated some meager wealth, originally intended for my own old age.

Now that my practice of *nien-fo* has reached fruition, I shall pass away on such-and-such a day and be reborn in a good realm; thus, this wealth is of no further use to me. I respectfully offer it to you.
The master replied, "What you have accumulated belongs to the entire community of shops; it is not the property of my family alone. How could I dare accept it? If it must be of no use to you,"

"Please perform meritorious deeds on my behalf. Mr. Wu was greatly delighted and handed over the keys to the caretaker, instructing him to go to the cellar at his residence and retrieve approximately one thousand *jin* of gold.
The caretaker distributed the funds among the great monasteries of Suzhou for the feeding of monks, and also shared the benefits with all the hermitages and guesthouses.
Once the meritorious work was completed, Mr. Wu, as scheduled, joined his palms in reverence and recited the Buddha’s name with a focused mind.
However, he passed away while seated. Among the monastics and laypeople from Wumen who escorted his coffin to cremation, there were tens of thousands.
Ba’an remarked: "This was an event from the Jiashu year of the Chongzhen era. I was lodging with Zhou Hengzhong at that time; his servant, Mr.
Lu, escorted the coffin back and spoke of it incessantly. This man’s conduct was similar to that of Zhang Bin."

If one recites the Buddha’s name with utmost sincerity throughout one’s life, it is possible that at the end one will accumulate great merit, and perhaps a Buddha or Bodhisattva will come to welcome one, leading directly to rebirth in the Western Pure Land; this remains to be seen.
Wu Shubo Received the Precepts at the Hour of Death and a Lotus Blossom Appeared:

Wu Shubo of Shangshe, Taicang, whose personal name was Minggong, possessed abundant wealth and had long been fond of doing good; he regularly participated in the society for the release of living beings, yet he was not particularly versed in the Buddha-dharma.
At over sixty years of age, he declared his desire to depart this life. Suddenly, he bathed and ordered that [monastics] be invited.
After the Dharma Master Yinchu of Longfu Temple had finished bestowing the Three Refuges and Five Precepts, he called out loudly for them to leave twice, then passed away with his palms joined.
A short while later, he opened his eyes again and spoke to his brother-in-law, Wang Yanke:
"I have just made the vow to forever sever ties with the mundane world and have courageously recited the name of Amitābha Buddha. I have leaped from beneath the bed and am now a lotus flower."

"A world of flowers. He reflected to himself, "What good deeds have I performed in my daily life to obtain this? He told the people of the world, "Exert yourselves! Having finished speaking, he asked for water and looked at his reflection.
In the middle of the night, he suddenly attained enlightenment, saying, "In this life I am Wu Shubo;
in a previous life I was Master Xu. He then cried out loudly, "How wonderful! and passed away. It is said that a wondrous fragrance emanated from his chamber.

The Retired Elder said, "The Buddha-dharma is one and the same. However, when one makes a vow at the moment of death and recites the Buddha’s name with focused intent, the merit will surely be more powerful than during ordinary times;

this is due to the difference between single-mindedness and lack of focus. During ordinary times, even if one recites the Buddha’s name tens of thousands of times with a distracted mind, it may not necessarily yield results.
Yet the butcher Zhang Shanhe attained rebirth in the Pure Land through ten recitations alone, and the hunter heard the bells upon his forked pole."
As for why a single utterance of the Buddha’s name causes a lotus flower to emerge:

it is because when death approaches and one stands before the realm of the dead, with the fires of hell before one's eyes, great terror cuts into the heart so deeply that there is no longer any object of attachment, nor any time for reflection.

Suddenly, the single invocation of the Buddha’s name is like a great crashing thunderclap or the collapse of Mount Tai; the karmic deeds accumulated during one's lifetime are dispersed like thickening mists.
When eggs are scattered, they are shattered to pieces; how could it be that the hells are not emptied and the Pure Land does not manifest?

Since Shubao converted the kalpa through his monastic life, he possessed innate roots from past lives. Approaching his death, he further received the precepts of refuge and recited the Buddha’s name with great vigor, whereupon a lotus flower emerged.
There is no reason to doubt this. For worldly people to exert themselves in this practice is indeed my final word. (Geng)
In the past, I once accompanied Shubao in the practice of releasing captive creatures. Wang Yan’eng, the former Minister of Rites, and his son both have biographies;
their accounts are most reliable based on what they saw and heard.
Wang Jian personally described his experiences in the netherworld after being mistakenly captured and subsequently returned to life.
Wang Jian of Wu Gate was a man of simple conduct and strict integrity. One day, he died suddenly during the day without any prior illness.

He was led by a green-clad attendant to the Netherworld, where Lord Yan interrogated him. It was determined that he had been summoned in error; the one who was actually to be taken was Wang Jian of Shandong. Consequently, Jian was permitted to return to life.
Upon leaving the Hall of Darkness, he beheld the hells where black flames shrouded the sky and the sounds of wailing were like the roar of thunder.

Three elderly monks were sitting in the lotus posture atop a great tree. Whenever the cries of suffering from the prisoners rose up in a tumultuous roar, he would sprinkle them with pure water, and the sounds would immediately subside.
Jian approached them to inquire who they were, and it was revealed that they were the three Great Beings: Avalokiteśvara, Samantabhadra, and Kṣitigarbha.
Jian was formerly acquainted with the Vinaya Master Baoguo Maolin, who was also in the underworld. His *kāṣāya* robe and mendicant’s staff appeared just as they did in his ordinary life.
Baiweng said: "Jian himself has a record of his return to life; here I have merely extracted the general outline."
Regarding the story of how a certain Zhou Xiucai attained the imperial examination by rejecting hidden wealth:
During the mid-period of the Ming dynasty, there was a scholar named Zhou [surname], whose given name was [name]. He was naturally upright and honest, yet his family was extremely poor.
He rented a single room at Han Jiatanzi near Loumen Gate; having dismantled an old stove, beneath a square brick at the base of the hearth, he discovered two yuanbao coins. His wife was overjoyed.
The Lord of Zhou said, "This is ill-gotten wealth; how could it be obtained? He took a brush and wrote upon the surface of the silver:
"If this is my wealth, it must come forth clearly. He then tucked it into his sleeve and went outside the Xu Gate, where he boarded a ferry boat, threw it into the middle of the stream, and returned.
A boatman witnessed this firsthand and immediately called out to a fisherman to cast a net and search for it. The fisherman retrieved the silver and hid it away separately.

When they were questioned, the two falsely claimed not to have seen him. They quarreled loudly and brought their dispute before the Magistrate. The Magistrate intended to impose punishment, but the two men confessed the truth.
He then had the fisherman arrested and immediately recovered the silver. Upon inspection, characters were found engraved upon it; he ordered it to be stored in the treasury.

That autumn, Zhou Gong sat for the provincial examination and ultimately passed. According to established custom, the local government held a "Little Deer-Crying Banquet" for every successful candidate, at which a plaque was presented with an accompanying gift of silver.
A hundred pieces of gold were placed before him; the two tablets of silver inscribed with characters were right there in front of Lord Zhou. The assembly was all struck with wonder.
Later, Cheng passed the jinshi examination.
The old man said, "This is what is called 'coming forth clearly. Lord Zhou was an eccentric of a bygone age; Cheng is an eccentric of our own time."
It is upright and square. It causes one’s fingers to touch dark objects; the blessings and favors will surely end here. How could there be another extraordinary event following this?
Everyone knows that the civil service examinations offer great benefit, yet when minor benefits appear before them, everyone cannot bear to let them pass by.
Alas! The "remote and impractical" teachings of the Duke of Zhou are truly the study of the Great Learning; how easy is it to reach such heights? This is Zhou Yixuan.
My master of ceremonies and fellow countryman—my master was an ancient gentleman who repeatedly spoke of this in public.

He noted that Mr. Gu Ruopeng of Kunshan, whose courtesy name was Jiuchou and whose style name was Xichou, served as the Minister of Rites (Zongbo) during the Chongzhen era; he had been publicly honored for his loyalty when he drowned while fulfilling his duties.
After the national upheaval of the *gapsin* year (1874), the entire family was immersed in grief and tragedy, vowing to die in martyrdom. His father, Un-sunju, starved himself to death.

When Master Sui (Sui-ung) was subsequently in Wŏnju, on the sixteenth day of the sixth month of the *binggu* year (1866), he was murdered by his colleague He Gun-yo and his body was submerged in the river.
Zhang Tiao-ding, styled Da-geng, was the Magistrate of Jianghua Ting and a student of the Master; he was fond of invoking the spirit medium (*jiji*).
The immortal suddenly descended, appearing as the Elder Rui. Da Geng asked him in astonishment, "When did you, Master, ascend the Mountain of the Way?
The spirit-writing replied, "On the sixteenth day of the sixth month, I was killed by the Deputy General He Juyao in the river."
Zhang asked, "What enmity do He and the Master have? The spirit-writing replied: "In a previous life, this old man was an elderly monk at Tiantai.
On my way back from begging for alms, I encountered a giant snake and struck it to death with my staff. He is the very reincarnation of that snake; thus we have met as karmic adversaries.
One must endure the fruits of one's own causes and effects. You may tell my two sons: by no means seek revenge. Zhang Gong immediately dispatched [the message].
When someone arrived in Wenzhou, they traced his whereabouts; everything matched exactly.
Baiweng said, "In the autumn of the Jichou year (1699), while I was at Kaiyuan Temple in Wuzhong, my fellow scholar of the inkstone, Wu Chunyou, met me there.
Because he had once served as the Magistrate of Yongjia, we spoke of Master Rui’s affairs. Chunyou said, 'This is my younger brother...'"

This is something I have personally experienced and witnessed with my own eyes. On the sixteenth day of the sixth month in the year of Bingxu, my younger brother hosted a farewell banquet for the Elder Rui at Jiangxin Temple under the moonlight.
The following morning, he reported that the Elder Rui had been killed. My brother summoned fishermen to search for him, but there was no trace or sign of him.
That night, I dreamed that the Elder Rui was standing in the water; I hurriedly commanded someone to support him [as he emerged].
As they boarded the boat, Ruiweng said, "In a previous life, I was an old monk at Tiantai. I mistakenly killed a snake, and now I must repay its life.
Because you were my disciple's disciple in a former existence, you have shown me such great kindness by arranging for my funeral affairs."
This was because there was a kinsman of his who lived beyond the mundane world. [The master said: "Tomorrow, simply seek him at such-and-such a bay; I shall be there.

Rising early the next morning, he inquired of a fisherman and indeed found that bay. He sought him out and found him, and then assisted him with all his strength as they returned to the ancestral cemetery at Kunshan.
Chunyou’s courtesy name was Guojie; he was a jinshi of the Gengchen year. Later, Junyao entered the sea.
He was also killed by others.
Zhang Yi was protected by divine grace in his preservation of integrity while facing peril. Mr.
Zhang Shouxian of Taicang, whose courtesy name was Cai, served his mother with supreme filial piety. In the Wuchen year of the Chongzhen era, the examination results had not yet been posted.

Previously, a friend dreamed that he was listed third on a placard, with the two characters "Filial Son" (孝子) noted beneath his name. Throughout his life, he had not placed much faith in Buddhism, but believed solely in Lord Guan.
On the first day of the New Year in the year of Yiyou, he dreamed that the Lord sent him a plaque inscribed with the words "Plaque of the Correct Qi of Heaven and Earth" (乾坤正氣匾) to his home.
The Duke was greatly pleased and spoke highly of him to everyone he met. Previously, many local elites and clerks in the prefecture had formed cliques to exploit the people.

Because the Duke possessed a nature that was upright and incorruptible, he reported their crimes to Qian Xisheng, the Prefectural Governor, who prosecuted them according to the law. Consequently, the petty scoundrels harbored deep resentment toward him.
They intended to take him prisoner. On the thirteenth day of the fifth month of that year, they took advantage of the chaos to waylay the Master on the road.

They seized him and carried him to the City God Temple, where they beat him mercilessly until his flesh and blood were mangled and putrefied. A young boy entered from outside and saw the City God shielding the Master with his own body.
The Master lay prostrate and motionless; the youths, believing he was dead, ordered a beggar to carry him away.
The official’s corpse was discarded beside the Guan Yu Temple in Xiao Jiaochang. At midnight, a monk in the temple said to his fellow residents, “Zhang Gong was a man of integrity.
His corpse has been cast away here; I fear it may be desecrated. We should carry it back to his home.

However, they had no other vessel to contain it, so they lowered the tablet inscribed with the characters “Qiankun Zhengqi” (The Righteous Qi of Heaven and Earth) onto a sedan chair and carried it to his residence.
He poured wine and gruel over him, whereupon his lips moved and he regained consciousness. After being nursed for less than half a month, he recovered; this was truly divine protection.
The following year, the ringleaders of the banditry were captured and executed by the hundreds in the marketplace.
Jie Xian said: "The Gong was my teacher when I was a student. He had never placed his faith in the monastics;

he respected only Master Konglin of West Temple in Kunshan, whom he regarded as a true monk. On the thirtieth day of the fifth month in the year Wuzi, as he drew near to death, he summoned me to his bedside and said:
'I have read all the Confucian classics, yet I alone have not applied myself to the inner scriptures.'"
Now my life is drawing to a close. Reflecting quietly upon the Buddha-dharma, I find that one point is most wondrous: at the critical juncture of birth and death, one must certainly not lack it.
It is regrettable that I have failed to reach this realization. Throughout my life, I have held biased views and committed verbal transgressions;

therefore, I specifically request several monks to perform the Liang Dynasty Repentance ritual for me once, so as to cleanse these defilements. Once the repentance is complete, I shall depart. For this reason, I bid you farewell.
At the hour of You (5–7 p.m.), he asked, "Is the repentance ceremony finished? When told it was complete, he passed away peacefully. Alas!

His teacher was stern, his spirit upright, and his nature inclined toward saving the world. Although he encountered hardship due to offending the petty crowd, from that time forward he vanished from human society;
he did not enter city gates nor meet with those in power, but fled into the wilds, where he ultimately attained [his goal].
Everything is returned to this. One knows that Heaven did not allow this jade-like man to fulfill his aspirations and integrity.

Although he had no affinity with the Buddha-dharma during his ordinary days, he attained repentance and awakening at the moment of his departure; these words are most excellent. Is this not because he possessed the seeds of wisdom from former lives, manifesting now in the body of a renowned scholar and official?
In the past, Xianbing attended by his teacher’s side, discussing the literary arts of antiquity and the present.
He was extremely receptive to my teachings. Whenever we discussed the Buddha-dharma, his face would turn red as he reproached himself for his failings.

When I manifested my resolve by wailing in mourning at the separate temple following the upheavals of the Jiashen year, burning my books, and leaving the household life, the Master instead praised me with the utmost fervor.

Later, when the lay practitioner Xu Menghong of Fuli requested that I clear the Plum Blossom Estate to establish Haizang Monastery, the Master sent a letter commending me, saying: [The text continues with the Master's letter.]
I, Yuan Da, believe that one who excels others should dwell in an eminent place.

My teacher—how could he have known that in future lives and subsequent worlds he would not become a great spiritual confidant within the Buddha-dharma? His friendship with Zhou was exceedingly profound; I know its beginning and end in full detail.

In the spring of the Gengwu year of the Chongzhen era, he withdrew from his retreat, contemplated breaking his fast, and ultimately committed suicide by hanging himself.
He was sleeping on the same bed as Zishao when he suddenly began to wail loudly in his sleep while reciting the Buddha’s name. Startled, Zishao asked for the reason, to which he replied:
"I dreamed that I arrived at the underworld. I saw an official of the Cao court carrying the registers of birth and death.

He said, "Three years from now, on such-and-such a day, I shall hang myself in my study. I wept and asked, "What crime have I committed to reach this state?

The official replied, "Karmic destiny is difficult to escape. I asked, "By what dharma might it be avoided? The official said, "Unless you observe the precepts, recite the Buddha's name, and practice with diligent effort, there may be some hope of avoidance.
He then said to Zishao, "Nephew, from this moment on, you must resolve to practice with single-minded devotion."

He then undertook a long fast and practiced the mindfulness of the Buddha with diligence morning and night for eight months. Later, his friends in the literary society clamored around him, saying, "This was merely a dream;
why allow yourself to be deluded by it? His resolve gradually wavered, and he finally broke his fast and ceased his observances.
In the spring of the Guiyou year, he unexpectedly bolted the door of his study and hanged himself. Counting back from that time, it had been exactly three years since his former dream.
The retired elder said: "In the year of Guiyou, while I was behind my curtains at Zishao’s Chuntiqi Hall, Yingzhi would frequently come to join me.
One day, he presented me with a Song-dynasty rubbing of a Huang Tingjian calligraphic work, saying, 'This was formerly in the collection of Grand Secretary Fan Changbai.

The son, with his hair disheveled and his face covered, wept and reported that he had already hanged himself as retribution. I was greatly shocked.

Outside the eastern suburbs of Macheng lived Master Qi, surnamed Wang. Having maintained a lifelong fast for three years, he suddenly contracted a malignant ulcer;

his entire body became festering and putrid, and the pain was unbearable. In his heart, he felt regret and withdrew from his practice. A close friend went to inquire after his illness and comforted him, saying: "You, sir, uphold..."

"You are a person who observes the fast; the Buddha and the heavens shall surely grant you silent protection. The King said, "I have observed the fast for three years, yet I have instead brought upon myself this evil retribution.
What benefit is there in fasting? His friend said, "If you do not desire this fast, may I buy it from you?"
Lord Wang asked, "How much shall I pay? The friend replied, "One silver coin per day; in three years, you shall have ten taels and eight mace.
Lord Wang was greatly pleased and immediately drew up a contract to receive the silver.

The next day he intended to break his fast and precepts, but that evening he suddenly saw two ghost messengers arrive and scold him fiercely, saying, "Because of your meager merit, your life-span and fortune were already exhausted ten months ago."
"It is exhausted. Because you observed the fast, it was extended until now; but now that you have sold it, the tally of your life has returned to your person.
I shall immediately issue a warrant to seize and compel you to comply. Wang Jun prostrated himself until blood flowed from his head, begging for a delay of one night.

He vowed to withdraw the silver and restore his lifelong practice of the fast. He urgently called upon his relatives and friends to retrieve the deed. A friend said, "I returned with the deed yesterday; I shall place it before the Buddha right now."
He prayed for the burning [of the corpse], whereupon the King-lord repented and died on the spot.
Ba-ung said: "In the year Bingshen, while I was reading the Tripitaka at the Xincan Hall in Macheng, the lay-devotees of the entire county came and spoke to me."
I personally witnessed this event.
The deity Fuzhu (Lord of Fortune) detested impurity and sacrilege, manifesting his spiritual power by dragging the temple [to its current location].
On the eastern side of Macheng, in Yizhou, there was a shrine to the deity Fuzhu that was extremely efficacious; its temple faced a river, separated from it by the water.
The townspeople were unaware of how to avoid it; dozens of urine buckets were lined up, and passersby voided their excrement right opposite the temple gate.

One night, the presiding deity exercised his supernatural power and pulled the temple around so that its back faced the river and its front faced the fields. To this day, it is known as the "Temple with the Reversed Wall."
The Retired Elder said: "Regardless of whether one is a monk or a layperson, one must cultivate refined conduct.

Whenever performing the acts of defecation or urination, one must choose a secluded place—either facing a wall or beside bamboo and trees. One must absolutely not face toward the stupas and temples of the Triple Gem, nor toward shrines of great or small deities;
even the void, the sun, the moon, and the constellations should be avoided. If one indulges in urination at will..."
To fall into [such error] incurs immeasurable sin. This matter is discussed most thoroughly within the Vinaya section.

The Case of Wu Zhanlou: A Record of His Cultivation and the Manifestation of Auspicious Signs in the Western Pure Land Wu Zhanlou of Taicang, in his later years, entrusted his household affairs to his two sons and devoted himself earnestly to the practice of the Pure Land. During the night watches, I personally heard the howling of ghosts. One evening, when the ritual documents were being burned, a multitude of ghosts leaped for joy and let out cries that echoed through the marketplace.
Min Yehua, whose courtesy name was Ruizhi, along with his fellow student Tao Zian and his servant, all defiled the ritual altar with impurities;
they were struck by a divine mallet and died.
I, Yu, out of compassion for those in the hidden realms, composed the *Dizang Chan-yi* (Ritual for the Repentance of Kṣitigarbha).

Once it was completed, my friend Wang Zhouchen resolved to have it carved into printing blocks. At the Kunsan Ancian Monastery during a period of the Dizang Repentance, I recorded these extraordinary events.
I also provided over a hundred taels of gold to have monks from Anchan Monastery in Kunshan assemble for a ritual of worship on behalf of my late wife, Lady Wu.
On the full moon of the ninth month in the year Wuzi, I established the date for the commencement of the rites.

Although the lay practitioner Zhang Zhansan lived more than twenty li away in Zhangpu and had not heard any news at all, on the night of the fourteenth, I dreamed that I arrived within Anchan Monastery and saw...

The ritual arena was solemn and orderly. The assembly of monks held incense burners and performed prostrations and repentance. When asked what they were doing, the presiding monk replied, "We are performing the Repentance for Deliverance from Hell.
After a short while, countless sinners appeared, their heads split open and their faces gashed;

their hands were severed and their feet cut off, with blood flowing over their bodies. Several hundred of them approached, and the monks sprinkled water upon them, saying, "Go forth to be born in heaven! The sinners [departed].
He immediately ascended into the air and departed. This occurred several times. Zhan-san was so terrified that he trembled.
The monk told him, "You must receive the five precepts before you can escape this peril. Zhan-san knelt and received them. Upon waking, he was greatly alarmed.
At dawn, he hurried to visit E-qiu to request a vegetarian meal and recount his dream. E-qiu said, "Today I have been meditating in my hermitage; Master Yuan has only just arisen."
He vowed to practice the *Dizang Chan* (Repentance Rite of Kṣitigarbha). Was this not the *Chudiyu Chanfa* (Repentance Method for Exiting Hell)? Upon hearing this, he was struck with awe and horror;
he immediately ran to the hermitage and vowed to serve as a laborer, never slackening until the end of his term.

In the winter of the Wuyin year of the Chongzhen era, my fellow calligrapher Zhang Erqiu—whose courtesy name is Liping—invited Master Dashi Zheng of Sanfeng to establish a Chan retreat at Qingliang An to the north of the mountain. After welcoming the Master into the monastery, Erqiu returned home. He had previously been eating meat, but having been moved by a dream, he observed the precepts and completed the full term of the retreat.

My fellow scholar Zhang Erqiu, whose taboo name is Liping, invited the Venerable Dashi Zheng of Sanfeng to the Qingliang Hermitage north of the mountain to commence a Chan period. Once the Master had been escorted into the temple, Erqiu returned.
The Master happened to eat chicken eggs and fresh fish that evening. That night, he suddenly dreamed that he had arrived at the gate of a hermitage.

There he saw the eight classes of devas, including the Nāgas, with green hair and protruding fangs, appearing in various strange forms. Fifty-six deities were departing from the gate in a great throng.
Approaching them in haste, he asked, "Where are you all, O Bodhisattvas, going? They replied, "We are the guardians of this site of practice (dharma-śālā). You have set a limit [for us]."

The Master returned home to eat meat, saying, "We no longer wish to protect the Dharma; we intend to disperse. Thereupon, Li Qiu knelt in prayer within a dream until his head bled, bitterly confessing his transgressions.
The various deities returned once more. From that time on, Li Qiu maintained the fast and observed the precepts for the remainder of the three-month period.
The retired elder said, "The following day, I spoke to my brother Erqiu, saying:

'This was a manifestation from the devas and dragons because you, my brother, have long promoted Buddhist affairs and accumulated profound merit; thus they showed you this dream to fulfill the appointed term.
Should your merit be slight, there would be no response, and the site of practice would surely disperse—would that not be perilous?'"
Gong Ermao Encouraged Goodness through Extensive Almsgiving; the Spirit Descended and Manifested Its Power to Gong Zhang.
Gong Zhang, styled Ermao, was registered in Hangzhou but grew up in the capital, Yanjing. By nature he loved to do good.

While airing his books, he discovered the "Treatise on Encouraging the Practice of Secret Merit" by the Lord of Zitrong. Upon reading it, he was filled with boundless joy and immediately made a vast vow to carve woodblocks for its printing.

It was circulated widely; as it pertained to the section on history (shǐ bù), he exerted all his efforts to print and distribute it throughout the various provinces, amounting to no fewer than several hundred thousand sheets.
Furthermore, through successive rounds of exhortation and conversion, within a few years the total reached over two million copies.

In the first year of the Kangxi era, while at the printing office in front of the hall, he saw the Emperor of the Underworld (Dìjūn) descending into the hall wearing a green robe and a jade belt during the day; he therefore painted [this image].

The people of the capital were moved by his offerings. Whenever there was a need for averting calamities, healing illness, praying for progeny, or seeking longevity, all would go to his home to make vows and receive his ritual seals;
after a single recitation of the scripture, Ermao’s prayers were invariably answered immediately.
Even the blind regained their sight, the insane were suddenly cured, divine images nodded in approval, and withered trees flourished once more—such were the various miraculous occurrences.
The Retired Elder said: "In the second month of the Gengxu year, when Lord Gong returned to Wulin following his period of mourning for his parents, he stayed at Lingyin Temple.
He personally recounted this to me and also provided me with a copy of the *Zibitong Baoying Lu*, which records numerous miraculous occurrences in full detail."
The Two Manifestations of Miracles at the Great Hall of Shushan:
At Baiyun Monastery on Mount Shushan in Fuzhou, which served as the site of practice for the founding patriarch Kuangren, there were many kinds of miraculous occurrences within the Great Hall.
During the Wanli era, a monk was walking in meditation outside the hall door one night when the incense burner and lamps, having been dim for some time, suddenly [flared up].
The monk Daiguang pushed open the temple door and saw a clay statue of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa standing beside him.

After he trimmed the lamp, it became daylight; the monk pointed out that this was the deity’s position. Furthermore, an official of the *xiao-lian* rank was seeking relief from the summer heat in the hall;
he spread his curtains before the Heavenly King and lay down naked. He dreamed of a spirit pressing a sword against him and rebuking him, saying, "You have shown sacrilege and arrogance!"
Upon reaching this point, he thought, "I will not heed these stellar deities; I shall strike you down with a single sword. At dawn, he opened his eyes and looked;

he found himself lying right before the Four Heavenly Kings, who held their staffs and swords. The filial and incorruptible man shrank his neck and broke into a sweat; he offered repentance and resolved to change his ways.

The retired elder said: "I had never stayed overnight at Sushan before. Ten years later, in the year Yisi (1235), at the earnest request of both monastics and laypeople, I preached the Dharma there and established a meditation hall.
I learned that there were many extraordinary matters within the monastery: pines planted beside Qinglong Mountain were the handiwork of the Patriarch;
the Dragon King had carved stone to form three great wells; and there was a half-width *kāṣāya* [robe]."
It completely covers the five peaks, forming the "White Cloud" (Baiyun) of its name. During the Yongle era, the Baiyun Temple was constructed with funds from the imperial treasury.
When a great bandit came to plunder it, he saw that all four sides were surrounded by thorn fences and that celestial soldiers were arrayed within. At dawn, he came to scout further.

The space was vast and shadowless. Thereupon, he turned his heart toward the Dharma and took refuge with Chan Master Daoben, while also donating his pirate ship to assist in the construction of the Great Hall.
Today, the walls are lined entirely with the planks of that ship. Those who sit upon lotus leaves reading the sutras were formerly pirates; this is the legacy of their remains.
Li Quanbu, whose courtesy name was Yaopu, obtained a male heir through the creation of a Buddhist image;
he maintained his integrity from beginning to end. Li Baichun, a jinshi of the Bingchen year, had never previously associated with monks.
Later, his three sons all died young. His father, Jingquan, invited the Elder Samadhi of Mount Hua to the Master’s residence for a vegetarian feast. From behind a screen, the Master...
Wang was startled and said, "This is the one I saw in a dream fifteen years ago. He then came forward, and they conversed with great intimacy.
During the meal, Wang asked, "Can you, Master, pray for an heir on my behalf? The Elder Mèi replied, "Your family’s merit and power are great;

He was about to commission two large incense statues of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, with an estimated cost of two thousand *jin*.

"If you can successfully complete this, I shall guarantee that you have a son," [the Master] said. The official agreed. He then contributed one thousand four hundred *jin*. The Master first conferred upon him a Dharma name, Dingzhi (Fixed Wisdom).
When the statue of Mañjuśrī was completed, a son was born; his milk name was Zhilang (Wisdom Boy), who is none other than the present-day Bǐnzhào.

The old man said, "Since the time of the great upheaval, you have kept your door closed to teach your sons and never appeared before government officials, steadfastly maintaining your integrity until nearly ninety years of age.
Suddenly, you saw banners, streamers, and ceremonial canopies approaching from the sky to welcome you. Thus it was.
Wearing his cap and sash, he passed away with a serene expression. He once said to Xian: "I have lost my family fortune through the chaos of war;
what was hidden in my underground vaults has been almost entirely plundered. I have nothing left but the meager merit I cultivated on Mount Hua, which no outsider can seize."
It is further said: "Rather than having had a home in years past but no son, it is better to have a son today but no home.
These are all instances where Master Gong has attained direct realization and found his own natural enjoyment.

He had a subordinate guest known as Zhu San-huzi (The Three-Bearded Zhu), who conspired with his servants to carry out various deeds. Master Baxin detested him deeply and intended to put him to death.
One day, he gave a visiting card to a servant, instructing him to deliver it to the county office and entrusting him with the task of taking Zhu San into custody.

The servant concealed the card and falsely reported that Zhu San had already been delivered to the jail. On another day, he again gave a visiting card with instructions to find Zhu San and report when his breath had ceased.
The servant once more falsely reported that Zhu San had already died in prison. Not long after, Master Gong fell ill; every day he saw Zhu San the Bearded coming to demand [retribution].
Fate! Because his family members were all in a state of confusion, they did not dare say that Zhu San was still alive; they prayed to the gods and sacrificed to the spirits every day.
Although the Old Lord saw with his own eyes what had happened, he could not explain it, and in the end, Zhu San captured him and killed him.
The Retired Elder said, "The Buddhist scriptures state that 'all things are created solely by the mind,' and further, 'the triple world is mind-only;
the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. Therefore, attaining Buddhahood or sainthood arises entirely from one's own mind; even falling into the three miserable realms arises from one's own mind.
Zhu San is still standing right there—what else is it that you, Master Bo, perceive? He replied, "Although Zhu San..."
Born from the hands of a family member, yet died within the heart of the Lord of the Earth (Bogong). External grievances can be resolved, but internal grievances cannot be resolved;
external ghosts can be sent away, but the ghost within the heart cannot be sent away.
The Lord of the Earth took Zhu San of his own mind and made him his own adversary, ultimately leading to his own destruction. This is not merely a matter of all things being mind-only.

What is the reason for this? In the end, Duke Bo has already returned to the underworld, while those three who were said to have "revived Zhu" are now strutting through the streets with tall crowns and wide sleeves;
will this not cause people to fall over in laughter for all eternity? The Patriarch said:
"Do not let the illness of the mind be that which is most difficult to cure. This is why Confucians are cautious in their solitude, and why the Chan school eliminates all seepage.
The elimination of the outflows (*āsrava*) is the foremost essential for spiritual practice.
An old man who had long suffered from illness rejoiced at the sudden departure of the "snake" of anxiety as his long-standing debts were cleared.
