He lent him one hundred taels of gold. Later, the filial and incorrupt (Xiao-lian) passed the jinshi examination and was appointed to an official post in the capital. For many years he did not return to his hometown. A neighboring elder suffered a sudden misfortune;
his family fortune was completely exhausted, and he fell ill, lying bedridden for a long time. He thought of the gold he had borrowed, harboring resentment in his heart.

Having been ill for so long, he could no longer maintain a fire for cooking, and his bitterness grew even more intense. Later, when Lord Zhou returned to his village, he suddenly recalled this past event.

He asked his family whether the neighbor’s old man was still there. When the family members described the man’s state of poverty and illness in detail, the official knit his brows and said, "This is my fault.
He immediately took the original silver and added another hundred pieces of gold, delivering them to the bedside. Upon seeing this, the sick man was filled with boundless joy.
With a "ka" sound, he spat out a snake, and his illness was immediately cured.
The old man said, "When I, your close friend, returned from Wumen to Kunshan with Master Hui, we moored our boat at Zhenyi.
At that time, the autumn waters were crystal clear; I saw a small shrimp or a water-insect at the bottom of the river, which rose up as a water bubble to the surface."
The face. A single blast and it immediately became a dragonfly. He blasted several more in succession. Next, he saw a creature floating up.
The Master playfully brought down a stalk of green reed upon it; the creature again exerted itself to float up, but was struck down by another stalk. This happened three times in succession.
Afterwards, the creature no longer floated up at all, but crawled horizontally onto the bank. Upon being blasted, it immediately became [a dragonfly].
The centipede: when the poison of a single thought arises, its physical form changes instantly. This is truly an extraordinary matter. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"When the mind-consciousness of sentient beings possesses inconceivable perfuming (*vāsanā*), there occurs inconceivable transformation.

The neighbor who became a snake due to long-standing resentment, and the aquatic insect that underwent instantaneous transformation due to extreme venom—these are all inconceivable matters within the mind-consciousness. What is more, [the text continues:]...
This refers to the inherent endowment (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*). Just as it is with evil, so it is with good. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"At the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta, one attains perfect enlightenment. Is it not here that one may achieve a vast and sudden awakening?
The Censor Ma Ji gave up his vegetarian fast due to misfortune and ultimately returned to the Way of the Gods.

The Censor Ma Jiashu of Pinghu, whose courtesy name was Peiyuan, was a jinshi degree holder of the Jiaxu year. His conduct was upright and pure, and he was refined and clean both inwardly and outwardly.
While serving an assignment outside the capital, two clerks from a certain office named Chen Mingfu and another arrived to collect outstanding grain taxes.
He instructed Park to die. Master Ma followed his advice. On the ninth day, while sweeping the grave, he suddenly saw two ghosts pleading their grievances.
Master Ma said, "This was the intention of my former office; it was not I. The ghosts replied, "As for this crime, we two were merely acting as substitutes; we were not the original offenders.
If you, Sir, would grant us a formal interrogation, we shall immediately clarify the matter. [Under the stroke of thunder, they could not remain.]

"Let it be settled," he said. Consequently, he died of grievous injustice. Now, although the two of us do not dare to demand his life, you, my lord, shall before long also depart this world to become the City God of Pufei.
Upon hearing these words, Lord Ma found them most abhorrent. He subsequently observed the fast and precepts, and under the guidance of the Elder Shiqi of Xuedou, he received the tonsure.
His dharma name was Xingqie, and his style was Sengxiang; he cultivated himself in pure and quietude.
He maintained this for twelve years, while residing at Huacheng Hermitage on the eastern shore of Jing Lake. He was on friendly terms with its abbot, Master Ciai.
One day, after eating chicken eggs due to a slight ailment, he suddenly saw two officials appear before him at midnight and said:
The Lord, having broken his vows of vegetarianism, was unable to remain; he was due to depart for Pufei on a certain day.
Lord Ma felt deep regret, and when the appointed time arrived, he passed away upon seeing the waiting officials with his own eyes.
The Retired Elder said: "Mǎ Péilǎo passed away as a manifest deity; it seems he did not fall [from the path].

However, his original aspiration lay in transcending the world, and thus he heard the teachings and practiced asceticism with great diligence. Who would have expected that he would fail to complete his fasts and observances and return once more to the way of spirits?
This truly proves that one must resolve to practice with a will as firm as iron or stone; one must not travel eighty *li* and then give up halfway at forty."

Qian Bo-yun, having studied Buddhism in her old age, ultimately attained rebirth in the West.

Dàcāng Qián Bǐng, courtesy name Bóyùn, was throughout his life exceedingly pure and virtuous. Having been appointed a District School Master (xuébō) in Pílíng for his proficiency in the Classics, he was promoted at the age of over seventy to serve as the Magistrate of Fùyáng.
His compassion and forbearance were beyond the ordinary. One day, he presided over the interrogation of a major thief.

The thief falsely claimed that he had been falsely accused by an enemy and pleaded with the Magistrate for his life. The Magistrate assumed a stern expression and said, "You set fire to people's houses and committed robbery and murder..."
The calculation was that the law should have resulted in the death penalty. Suddenly, the thief sprang up, seized the official’s desk, inkstone, and brush, and hurled them at the official’s chest.

The official fell to the ground in pain. The officials gathered around and beat the thief mercilessly. The official scrambled up; with one hand he rubbed his chest and with the other he stopped the officials, saying, "Do not hit him!
Do not hit him! It does not hurt here. Those who heard this collapsed with laughter. Later, he returned to his hometown.
He was deeply committed to his practice and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily. He further composed commentaries upon it, gaining a profound mastery of its meaning and intent.

At the time of his death, his mind attained spiritual penetration. He spontaneously composed a funeral inscription and verses of praise. He then instructed that "cooling water" be brought for him to drink quickly and cleanse his intestines and stomach.

When asked where the cooling water was located, he replied, "It is the water from the放生池 (Fangsheng Chi, or 'Releasing Living Beings' Pond). Once it was brought and he had finished drinking, he joined his palms in reverence.
He said, "By the power of the Buddha, I have gone directly to the Pure Land of Clarity and Voidness. He sat peacefully and passed away with a joyful countenance.
Ba’eng said, "You were my father’s close friend. The entire Pengcheng clan has been my lifelong companion. When the upheaval of the Jiashen year occurred, I left home to become a monk;
you likewise retired to the countryside to study the Buddha-dharma. Upon arriving at Taiping Hermitage, you inquired about the Dharma, and I showed it to you."
He was extremely devoted to the *Vajra Commentary*. At the time of his departure, he displayed a state of liberation and there were extraordinary signs.
Is this not clear evidence that one who has practiced virtue throughout a lifetime attains realization at the end of their path? Sun Sansi passed the provincial examination again in the Jiyou year;
such is the unfailing retribution Heaven bestows upon the virtuous.
Huang She-liu was a man of profound devotion to the Western Paradise who vowed to depart for Sukhāvatī at a fixed time.
His courtesy name was Huang She-liu; his given name was Yìshèng, and his style name was Zǐyǔ. He had long been an eminent friend within the Lotus Society (*liánshè*).

Although born of noble lineage and possessed of extensive learning, he was pure in conduct and deeply cherished the teachings of Yunqi. The entire family practiced with singular diligence. When he was recommended and appointed as a magistrate in Sichuan—

In the new capital, he governed the people with compassion, and his reputation for benevolence spread far and wide. It was passed down that he would provide meals for the monks in the county hall, personally attending to the serving of spoons and bowls and distributing food with his own hands, followed by prostrations.
Those who heard of this found it strange. Later, when the Xian rebels invaded Western Sichuan, they slaughtered everyone in their path, and corpses were piled as high as mountains.
Several thousand monks, moved by the governor’s vow of merit, ascended the city walls, struck wooden clappers, and recited the Buddha’s name throughout the middle of the night.

The Buddha’s voice thundered through the heavens. When the rebel Xian asked why this was so, the local people replied, "Because Magistrate Huang has always loved goodness, he provides meals for the monks.

The monks strike the wooden board and recite the Buddha's name to guard the city. The rebels were instructed not to cause disturbance; thus they passed by in silence, without startling even the chickens or dogs.

Later, he returned to his fields and steadfastly cultivated the Pure Land practices. In the tenth month of the Jihai year, his illness grew somewhat grave. I— [text ends] — (Note: The provided source text is incomplete at the end. The translation reflects the portion available.)
When his elder brother-in-law, Wang Yanweng, braved the cold to visit his cottage, he found Amitābha images displayed on all four walls, as he had made preparations for his western departure.
He requested that I confer the Bodhisattva precepts upon him during the third watch of the night; I then gave him an exhaustive discourse on the pure contemplation of mind-only.
Master She said, "My spiritual clarity grows ever stronger and my vows grow ever firmer; I am confident that I will certainly be reborn in the Western Land.
The following morning, he took his leave, stipulating that he would surely depart on the eighth day. Counting the days, it was indeed no more than that.

Wang Fengchang, whose ancestors had accumulated merit over generations and whose line of imperial degrees continued unbroken from the time of Grand Secretary Wang Xianshou (Wang Xijue), styled Jingshi—the chief minister during the early years of Emperor Shenzong—was indeed illustrious and prominent. Yet...
Throughout his life, he never took a second wife. His service at court, his eminent reputation, and his great merit in establishing the heir apparent are recorded in the national annals;

what follows here is but a brief record of one or two anecdotes from his private life as a resident of his home village. The Duke was by nature humble, respectful, gentle, and kind, yet he alone maintained strict discipline over his subordinates.

He favored simplicity and would not allow his servants to wear fine silks or brocades. Once, when some of his servants were engaged in a physical altercation with others and stepped forward to intervene, their skin was wounded.
The Duke must have said: "Even a single dog in the Chancellor’s residence is regarded with special consideration; how much more so a human being? He would surely first reprimand his servant.

The Sanskrit characters were neither large nor small; he inscribed them all upon his forehead to maintain their protective power. In his later years, he commissioned artisans to paint images of the Bodhisattva using gold and silver pigments.

His late father served the Buddha with refined sincerity and repeatedly experienced miraculous responses.
His father’s courtesy name was Mèngqiú, his style name Kāiyún, and his sobriquet Ānxīu Jūshì. Having entered the local academy in his youth, he initially did not place much faith in Buddhism;

One night, he dreamed of a man dressed in black who begged for his life, saying: "Tomorrow I shall come to your house; you must pray that I be spared."
"I have not escaped calamity," he said, waking up and telling his wife. His wife said, "Wait a moment. Just then, a tenant farmer caught a giant turtle, as large as a pot lid;

"Could what I dreamed last night be this? he asked, urging that it be released. The light replied, "A creature must possess spiritual intelligence to be able to manifest in a dream;

That very night, the man’s belly ruptured and he suffered diarrhea; within three days, he died from the diarrhea.
The retired elder said: "He was a fellow student of my friend Hong Zhangxiong, with whom I shared my inkstone.

Again, I saw the Lord Yama say: "Your retribution as a snake is not yet exhausted; how can you seek death for yourself? You must once more become a snake to exhaust your past karma.

In Hankou, there was a butcher who did not heed the monk’s exhortations and subsequently suffered a miserable retribution.

The monks earnestly urged him to purchase the dog and set it free, but the butcher stubbornly refused. He then said, "You and this dog have a karmic enmity from past lives;
I cannot save you. He joined his palms and prostrated three times before the butcher.

That night, as the butcher slaughtered the dog and lifted it toward the cauldron, boiling water suddenly splashed onto his chest. He died seven days later, his body completely perforated by the burns. The people of Hankou were moved by this.
They then pooled their funds to construct the present Fangsheng Hermitage. Ba’weng said,

The Pig of Gaoyou Who Exchanged Her Body for a Mat and Ultimately Repaid Her Debt:
An old village elder in Sanduo Town, Gaoyou, raised a sow that produced many offspring. Over the years, he grew wealthy.
Suddenly, he dreamed of a man who said to him, "I have returned my old debt to you for many years; I owe you only one shoulder-width of reed matting. Upon waking, he was filled with doubt.
It so happened that news arrived that a sow had died. Out of pity for its past service, the village elder ordered his son to bury it.
As the son held a spade and was just beginning to dig a pit by the riverbank, a boat made of reed matting suddenly arrived. When asked what he was burying, the son replied—
A dead pig was facing him. The boatman said, "Although the pig died of its own accord, it is still fit to eat. He then exchanged it for a shoulder-load of reed mats.
Zizi returned with the reed mats on his head, and his father sighed with great admiration.
The Retired Elder said: "This was personally witnessed by my disciple West Hall Zhuoyuan, who recounted it to me.
The repayment of karmic debts is precise to the smallest detail; it is both laughable and terrifying."
The Butcher of Penglang Town Immediately Encounters the Retribution for His Deeds.
In Penglang Town of Dacang, there was a butcher whose profession was slaughtering oxen. Having purchased oxen from north of the Yangtze River, he returned as the year drew to a close.
When he asked his wife for meat to eat, she replied that there was none. The butcher, filled with indignation, took up a knife and cut out the ox’s tongue to give to his wife.
While cooking, he went into his room and sat down; facing his wife, he adjusted his dressing table and looked at his reflection, using a knife to trim and scrape his eyebrows.
Suddenly, the rope of the window-lattice snapped and fell, splitting his head in two, and his life ended instantly. This was recounted by the mouths of all the townspeople.
The Dao-ren of Jinling’s Huashan Mountain lived as a man of the Way, yet he disregarded the laws of cause and effect.
Greedy and gluttonous, he misappropriated the temple storehouse. Later, he drowned in the Jiegong Pond in front of his gate.
Not long after, he appeared in a dream to the Acharya Dazhao and said: "I have already become a donkey. Tomorrow, I shall..."
When he went to pay off his debts at Changzhu, it was indeed dawn. He called for the monk Ju, who then hurried forward with great speed;
he repeatedly went to the storehouse to demand food, his habitual tendencies remaining as they were. After several years of repaying his debts, he died once more in the pond.
The Retired Elder said: "This is a precedent from Mount Hua that everyone who knows the One Vehicle understands. Since cause and effect are so manifest, how can one not stand in awe?
Cao Han nearly slaughtered a city, yet he encountered circumstances and was saved."
Liu Xixuan of Suzhou, courtesy name Yushou and style name Xincheng, was a jinshi of the gengxu year. He initially served as a professor in Luling, then accepted an invitation to Yunnan;
while passing through Qianzhong on his way back, he moored his boat at a post station. There, he dreamed of a tall and imposing man who told him:
"I am Zhu Jiangcao Han. During the Tang dynasty, I was a merchant who passed by a temple and saw a Dharma Master there."
He ascended the high seat and preached the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections* of the Buddha-dharma. I resolved to provide a vegetarian feast for one hall and sat through the lecture on one occasion.
Because of these roots of goodness, throughout my life I served as a minor official and never failed to hold office.

Reaching the beginning of the Song dynasty, I was promoted to the rank of General of the Left, named Cao Han. While campaigning against Jiangzhou, which did not surrender for a long time, he became enraged and slaughtered its inhabitants. From that time onward—
"In life after life I have been a pig, subjected to slaughter by men. The place where you, sir, have moored your boat is precisely my place of death.
In a short while, I shall be the very first to be slaughtered; having met you by karmic destiny, I pray that you will deign to show me compassion and save me.
Master Liu sprang up and called his servant to look at the bow of the boat; it was indeed a butcher’s gate. A moment later, the gate opened and a pig was carried out, its cries shaking the earth.

Liu Chang purchased [the manuscript] and transported it back to the Western Garden within the Changmen Gate. He called for Cao Han, who responded immediately. The Master (Gong) published the *Yinyuan* extensively;

The retired elder said, "A pig’s karma is heavy and its nature is dull; how could it manifest a dream? That which was able to manifest the dream was actually the residual blessing from listening to the sutras.

The Duke recounted the matter to me. When I arrived at Xiyuan, I still managed to see this pig; its body was well-groomed and clean.

"When you witness others being slaughtered in your daily life, what Dharma can save them? Cao Han replied: "Whenever they are being butchered and dismembered, their suffering is unbearable;

At Wujiang Road, the great grievance of Cong was righted like falling snow;

He exhausted his family fortune of several hundred thousand in almsgiving (*dāna*). At forty, he did not marry again.

[The heat] at the crown of the head remains hot for several days. The retired official [Wang] Wen said:

For ghosts, they emerge from the abdomen; for animals, from within the kneecaps; and for those in the hells, from the soles of the feet. This is the established rule for their placement.

For when the mind dwells in meditative stillness, it is light and pure, coalescing within; whereas when the emotions are obstructed by love and hatred, they are necessarily heavy and turbid, adhering to external objects.

That which is light flies beyond the clouds without sinking; that which is heavy plunges into the stones without being lifted. Accumulated over a single lifetime, this is self-verified at the very end.
Layman Xiao Jiang cultivated his practice for fifty years until the top of his head grew hot;

Every time he ate, regardless of whether the food was fish or meat, he would first wipe the Buddha’s mouth and call out, "Buddha, Father, you eat first."

You must blow it. Do not let it be flat. This is the conch of the Dharma. You must sound it. Do not let it be faint. This is the voice of the Tathāgata. You must hear it. Do not let it be unheard. This is the speech of the Bodhisattvas. You must listen to it. Do not let it be ignored. This is the teaching of the Arhats. You must follow it. Do not let it be neglected. This is the perseverance of the steadfast. You must persist in it. Do not let it be discouraged. This is the

He said, "My father was from Jixian; his name was Gan. At eighteen, he served as a grain-tax collector (*liángzhǎng*). He first collected three hundred taels of silver from these three men and diverted it for personal use.
Furthermore, he brought harm upon them. Therefore, I have come to collect this debt. Having finished speaking, he again shook with convulsions and fell into a trance.
I led the assembly in sprinkling pure water and reciting mantras, and further distributed *hu* of food, preparing several large portions for the various quarters.
The paper talisman was burned. When the monk saw the ghost, it clapped its hands and led him away; he then immediately regained consciousness.
The old man said, "A son repays his father's debts—this is the natural order of things. Even as a monk, one cannot escape such debt."
"One must not betray others in such a manner.
Second, the two *xiao-lian* (exemplary scholars) who insulted and treated with contempt the God of Literature suffered the loss of both their person and their official emoluments:
Li Yu of Fuzhou and Wang Yuan-sheng. Having repeatedly presented themselves before the Imperial Academy (*chun-guan*) without success, they were deeply embittered. First...
Suffering from a hangover, he went to the Temple of Zitrong. Seeing the image of the Lord of the Emperor (Dijun), he pointed at it and reviled it, saying, "I shall no longer serve you!
Why do you still remain here receiving offerings? He then ascended the divine throne and pushed the image with all his might;

the pedestal was overturned and shattered into pieces. The two men returned home and developed a high fever. The Lord of the Emperor possessed them and cursed them in great pain, saying, "You two mad scholars! Previously..."
"In this world, you have performed but a small amount of merit. The High God has rewarded you with filial piety and integrity, and your family fortune is already more than sufficient.

Why do you act so recklessly and insolently as to destroy my image? Your wickedness has reached its ultimate limit! You shall be immediately delivered to the Underworld for interrogation and punishment.
The family members were struck with terror; they spent several nights consecrating and erecting a sacred image, yet in the end, he died without being saved.
The retired elder said: "In the year of Bingwu, while I was in Min, I personally heard this matter.
Later, I inquired of the monastics in Fuzhou, and they all spoke with one voice, confirming it to be true and beyond dispute."
Two *xiao-lian* (exemplary scholars) from Macheng were arrogant toward Dizang and received retribution for their deaths.
One of them believed in the Buddha, while the other was contemptuous of the Buddha; they were both reading together in a Dizang Hall when a relative brought dog meat as a gift.
The believer rubbed [the meat] away, saying, "Do not play such a joke. The arrogant one said, "A great man does not..."

Upon seeing this minor transgression, those who were faithful fled in a panic to the outside of the gate, while those who were arrogant instead ascended the Buddha’s seat, intending to mockingly offer meat to the Bodhisattva.
Just as they raised their chopsticks into the air, they suddenly gave a shove that sent them crashing to the ground; they fell prostrate and died instantly.

A short while later, the filial and upright scholar from outside the gate also died. They arrived together at the Netherworld, where they saw the arrogant man being subjected to all manner of tortures—whipping, flogging, and a hundred other punishments.

He was bound with a neck-shackle, and flames erupted from the shackle, burning his entire body until it was charred and ruined. The Lord of the Netherworld said to the believer, "Because of your faith, you ought not have come here.
I have caused you to come so that you may bear witness to the suffering there and transmit this knowledge to the world of the living.
He then issued an order for him to return to the realm of the living, whereupon he revived.

The Elder Ba’eng said: "Master Sibu of Aengnyan and Master Sindang of Gokmun personally recounted that those who have long been disrespectful toward the spirits and Buddhas have all met with perilous retribution.
Yet worldly people do not realize this; they often regard the spirits and Buddhas as mere absurdities."
They immediately treated [the sacred objects] with contempt and insolence, thereby bringing calamity upon themselves; it will be too late for them to regret this.

A commoner of Jianchang, surnamed Wang, who had long been unfilial in his conduct, was struck dead by a thunderbolt outside the South Gate of Jianchang Prefecture on the [blank] day of the seventh month in the year of Yisi.

Three Treasures (Sambhoga-kāya, Dharma-kāya, and Nirmāṇa-kāya). A small commoner of Jianchang. Surnamed Wang. His habitual behavior was unfilial. On a certain day in the seventh month of the Yisi year.
Every day he purchased beef and had it cooked in the monks’ cauldron at Jōdo-ji Temple.
While the royal official was scraping the fibers from a melon by hand for the child, the child suddenly saw a woman dressed in crimson robes enter the room carrying a large mirror on her neck;
she pointed her finger at the official, whereupon the official immediately knelt down. He then saw a thunder god strike him with a mallet, and a great flame erupted.
As he went outside, he let out a cry; the king’s body and face turned entirely black, and he died standing. On his back was a line of characters that no one could decipher.
Ba’eng said, "In the autumn of this year, I happened to be at Jingyun Temple in Jianchang; it is not more than a few *li* from Jingtusi."
The arrow struck him; there was no one among his attendants who did not go to see it. This became known throughout the city, both inside and out.
[I realized] that eating beef was a sin, so I seized the opportunity to speak to Yan Yu-huan and Ti Tai about it. Consequently, a prohibition against slaughtering oxen was established.
Those of Yongcheng who defile stupas and temples immediately meet with extraordinary calamities.
The Tianfeng Pagoda is located within the city of Ningbo. In the ninth month of a certain year, several commoners carried wine and meat onto its summit, shouting and reveling.
One man even urinated and defecated at the pagoda’s entrance. At that time, the autumn sky was bright and clear, when suddenly a thunderbolt struck him.
A man fell from the pagoda and died; cups, plates, jars, and goblets flew like stars. The others all threw them down at the base of the pagoda, and the pagoda followed the flames of the fire.
It has now been restored and repaired. Furthermore, the pagoda of the Venerable Master of Four Ming Realms, the Great Master Fazhi, is located at Yanqing Temple.

While a group of young students were competing in their skills within the temple, one of them urinated upon the pagoda. A bystander was startled and said, "The spirit of the pagoda is not [to be trifled with]!"
He remarked, "It is despicable. The monk departed several hundred years ago; since his remains have long since decayed, what spirit could there possibly be? He then threw himself into the water.
Suddenly, he was seized by a fit of madness and drew a knife to commit suicide. His companions supported him as they boarded the boat, but he plunged back into the water and died.

The retired elder said: "Qian Xisheng, the younger brother of the Prefectural Governor, recounted that Chen Xiang, who had been a butcher of dogs, relied on his wickedness and did not feel remorse; thus he manifested himself to receive retribution.
Among my disciples in the prefecture, there was Qian Dengjiu. One of his servants, named Chen Xiang, would enter the inner quarters daily to perform labor. Secretly—"

He was a butcher of dogs. Although I exhorted him morning and evening with bitter words and earnest advice, he ultimately did not change his profession. One day, he ate fresh pufferfish; the poison took effect, and he suffered such agonizing distress that he was on the verge of death.
A physician advised that consuming a mixture of excrement and water might save him. Just as Chen Xiang was about to reach the latrine, a snake appeared.
He devoured excrement in great quantities; ultimately he was not cured. He died wailing with the mournful cries of a dog.
Xiong Jina protected the Dharma with such fervent devotion that he obtained a successor within the scheduled period at Nan-kang and Jian-chang.
Xiong Shilong, styled Jina, was the younger brother of the Censor-in-Chief Qingyu Gong, whose name was De-yang.

He was a son [of the lineage]. He protected the ancestral seat of Yunju for generations. When Master Yishu wished to invite Master Zhuanfu to reside at Yunju, he charged his son with the arrangements.
Zhi-na took personal responsibility for the monastery, serving with the utmost sincerity; he procured various household items at a cost of five hundred strings of cash.
Coincidentally, his wife was pregnant at home. Master Zhuanfu said, "Since you protect the Dharma in this manner, the Buddhas and Patriarchs will surely grant [the child] their blessing."
A male heir was born. Ji Na established a covenant, saying: "If [the deity] manifests its spiritual power to protect the Dharma, the son must be born on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month;
the seventh or ninth days shall not count. Later, when the son was born to Xiang Yu Guo on the eighth day of the twelfth month, it did not deviate by even a hair's breadth.
The retired elder said, "I resided at Yunju for ten years, and Ji-na protected the Dharma from beginning to end.

When I moved to Huangmei, I stayed at the Fourth Patriarch’s monastery for three years, and it was only then that you passed away. Your sincere devotion to the Dharma is rare indeed among ten thousand."
How lamentable!
The scholar Gu, who returned to life after his crane had transformed, has sought out and verified these facts:
in the *bingzi* year of the Chongzhen era, the scholar Gu of Wuxi was staying at Ba’en Temple in Changgan while lodging for the provincial examination.
She was resting during the day when she suddenly dreamed that she had become a white crane soaring through the air.
Her heart was filled with great joy as it flew to the edge of the Yu Hua Terrace. There she saw a house with a hall and rooms of magnificent beauty, its nameplate elegant and refined;
she memorized every detail. She flew into the inner chamber and saw several women surrounding a woman in labor. Suddenly, the crane became dizzy and fell into a basin.
The entire family celebrated with joy. Startled, he thought to himself: "I came here originally for the provincial examination; if I were to become someone else's heir, I would surely die.
He then cried out loudly and woke up, only to find his servants surrounding him, weeping for a long time. The following day, the scholar recorded the couplet on the door plaque.

He ordered his servants to search for them, and they were all found exactly as described. It turned out to be a wealthy man who had been childless since middle age. Upon hearing this, the old man was overcome with grief;
he went to the temple, recognized the scholar, and presented him with a generous gift, saying, "It was because of my own meager merit that I could not invite you, sir.
He then departed, weeping bitterly.
The retired elder said, "I was also in the southern region when the examination took place, and I witnessed and heard of this with great astonishment.
Elder Huang Feng, through his practice of goodness, moved the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara) to grant him a son, thereby establishing a great name and integrity.

This was Huang Yunsheng of Jiaxing; his father, having difficulty obtaining a son in his middle years, diligently performed acts of merit and assiduously recited the *Baiyi* (White-Robed One) mantra."

One night, the Master suddenly dreamed that a Great Being (Mahāsattva) brought him a child and presented him, saying: "I have observed your diligent suffering in reciting the sutras and practicing virtue;
I have sought out an exceptionally fine scholar for you. You must raise him well. Initially, the child was named Jinyao (Golden Radiance), who became a renowned scholar.

Later, his name was changed to Chunyao (Pure Radiance). During the Guiwei year of the Middle Cycle, he passed the jinshi examination. In the Yiyou year, moved by indignation over the changes in the world, he [joined] with his younger brother, Wei Gong.
He hanged himself outside the North Gate, within the Buddha Hall.
Bai Weng said, "In the past, at the examination grounds, I frequently encountered Wei Yunsheng; he was truly a gentleman of jade and gold.
Later, he achieved fame as a jinshi, yet the Great Master (the Emperor) merely called him 'a fine scholar. In antiquity, it was said that the value of a scholar is determined by Heaven."
He took it upon himself as his own responsibility. Like one who harbors a gem within, his talent and character were preeminent, and his integrity and loyalty were chillingly resolute;
he was truly a fine scholar.
When Wu Xiachou reached the end of his service to his sovereign, he burned his body, and his spirit ascended to heaven.

Wu Zhongluan, courtesy name Luanzhi, style name Xiashou, was a native of Piling. He had long been a renowned elder of the scholarly community. At over sixty years of age, he passed the jinshi examination.
He first served as the Magistrate of Changxing and was subsequently promoted through various ranks until he reached the position of Judicial Commissioner (Sizhe) in Guangxi.

During the Shenyi and Youyi years [1645–1647], due to the upheaval of the state, he fled to Mount Zhou. There, he would often reflect to himself: "My disciple Li Zhongda and my fellow student Ma Suxiu..."
"Both have died maintaining their integrity. I am now nearly eighty years old; if I were to fall ill and pass away suddenly, would it not be as if I had betrayed these two men?
I shall seek a place of death that is clear and pure, so as to show myself to those who know me. At that time, the Master was within the fortress of Zhou Shan City.
He resided within the Confucian Temple. First, he gathered firewood to construct a shrine, in which he placed a high seat.
Upon hearing that the city had fallen, he took the sacred tablet in his arms, ascended the shrine, sat down, and ordered his servant to set the fire; it was consumed in an instant.

Not long after, he descended as a spirit-medium at the home of Zhang Danyu in Pilu and declared that after his body was cremated, his spirit would ascend to become a green-clad messenger of the Yuxiao Palace. He then composed a poem.
"Several of his writings remain in the world; there are eighty instances where he burned his body for the sake of you, my lord. Even now, when I recall those words, I still shed tears.
Ba’eng said, "In the eighth month of Bingwu, I returned from Caoxi and arrived in Qianzhou, where I met with your fourth son."
The Duke resided together with him at Dongxi Temple, where he witnessed firsthand the woodblock carvings recording these events in detail. The elder Mr.
Shi, having long sponsored monks for the Jiu-yuan (Nine-Distance) fast, was moved by the fact that his son, Shi Da-cheng, had become the Grand Champion and National Scholar;
thus he bestowed upon him the style name Lian-an. It was said that in a previous life, he had been a monk at a certain temple in Ningbo, using the name Da-cheng.
Whenever Master Si collected rice from the alms bowl and found the communal rice bucket shallow, he would invariably go to Mr. Shi’s house to fill it before returning to the temple;
this became his constant practice for many years, though the exact duration is not recorded. Mr. Shi, a man of long-standing virtue, kept a large bowl to hold rice as an offering for the Buddha.
Later, he used it to serve as a rice bowl for five generations. One day, he suddenly saw the monk Da-cheng entering his room; though he searched for him, no trace remained.

He then established a hermitage and named it Da-cheng. He maintained the *tai-zhai* (embryonic fast), and although he achieved the highest honors in the imperial examinations, his observance of the precepts remained as before.
A monk from his previous life had become his dharma friend, and they continued to accompany one another as companions.
The Retired Elder said, "In the past, while I was at Shiting Temple in Hongdu, I read your poem which says: 'Long observing the fast, I do not suffer for having no fish;
entering the womb and passing through the intermediate state, my true nature remains undeluded. My Daoist bones and Chan mind remain as they were, unchanged by karmic maturation.'"
The true efficacy is manifest before our very eyes.
Master Yang saved people through his skillful speech, thereby bringing warmth and wealth to his household.
He was a commoner from Shihu in Suzhou, surnamed Yang. Originally living in extreme poverty, he engaged in thievery; however, he learned that an elderly woman possessed a small amount of...

While she was away, a man stored his belongings and entered the room through a breach in the wall during the dead of night. He saw the old woman working at her spinning wheel by the lamp and hid behind the bed to watch her.
Suddenly, he saw a blue-faced ghost repeatedly encircling the woman’s head with a noose. The woman immediately stopped spinning and sighed, saying, "What hardship is it to live for others?
It would be better to hang myself. She then rose, sought out a rope, and fashioned a loop from a rafter. Climbing onto a wooden stool, she hanged herself.
The ghost pushed over the machine and seized her feet with both hands to pull them down. The thief was terrified and, forgetting that he was a thief, cried out loudly, "Quickly save me!
The old woman had three sons who rushed in together through the door; they hurriedly rescued her, and the mother did not die.
She bowed her head and thanked the thief, saying, "Kind man, kind man! Yet in such a dark night, why have you come here yourself?"
"Come here! When the thief heard these words, he was suddenly awakened and cried out, "Alas! Alas! I am truly a rebel against humanity.
Because of extreme poverty, I became a petty thief, hoping merely to stay alive. Just now, seeing the blue-faced ghost harming your mother, I could not help but cry out in horror.
I beg you to forgive my crime; it would be enough if you would simply release me and let me go. The three sons said, "You have saved our mother's life. This is a great [deed]..."

The benefactor thought, "I must surely repay this kindness," and so he invited him to stay overnight as a hospitable guest. At dawn, he presented him with ten taels of gold and exhorted him to become a good person.
The thief was moved by realization and changed his ways; taking the gold as capital, he managed trade and accumulated a fortune of a thousand taels.
Shihu referred to him as a "minor wealthy householder."
The Retired Elder said: "This concerns events from the final years of the Ming dynasty. Monk Shihu has recounted them repeatedly and in great detail.
As for the youth Wu of Jinwang, who encountered a transcendent and cherished his life, he missed a marvelous opportunity.
This youth Wu of Jintang was a devoted believer in Lüzu; every day he went to the shrine of the Immortal to pay his respects, hoping to obtain a vision of him. (Wu) Weng.
On the evening of the thirteenth day of the fourth month in the fifth year, I dreamed that a deity told me:

"Tomorrow is the birthday of the Patriarch. He who wears a purple yang-jin cap and a blue *huang* robe is the Patriarch Lü. Do not let this opportunity pass; go early tomorrow morning to wait for him. It was indeed so. I then prostrated myself, entreating him with great earnestness to grant me deliverance.
At first, the Patriarch firmly refused, but finally he led me to the top of a city wall and commanded me to close my eyes. With his left hand...
He held up an umbrella, and with his right hand grasping the sleeve of the Patriarch’s robe, he immediately ascended into the air. After a short while, the sound of a surging tide roared.
Opening his eyes to steal a glance, it appeared as though they were floating and flying across a vast ocean. Lüzu said, "Do you truly wish to seek immortality?
You may leap into the water. He hesitated, and the Patriarch said, "It was to be expected that you have the bones of a commoner," and struck him once on the neck.
He fell [into the water] and was found on a sandbar in Lake Dongting. It took him three months as a beggar to reach Wumen.
Ba’eng said, "Whether seeking immortality or seeking the Buddha, one must employ the primary thought; if one hesitates even slightly, one will surely retreat.

As for the Second Patriarch standing in the snow and severing his arm, and Master Jing’ai gouging out his eyes because the Tang Emperor Wu suppressed the teachings—[these were acts of the primary thought].
His entrails hung from the tips of the trees. Could the second thought have caused this? When Master Wu sought immortality, he encountered it yet failed to attain it;
was it not the second thought that brought him harm? This was personally witnessed and recounted by my friend, Layman Menghe.
A blind man, harboring a malicious intent, was about to rob and kill his own life when he suddenly collapsed at a well-shed on a road in Poyang County, Ruzhou. Beside it lay a desolate grave.
On the first day of the sixth month of the Gengzi year, a merchant entered the shed for water and saw a blind fortune-teller with a boy acting as his guide inside. He then ordered [the boy]...
He performed a divination. Having finished the calculation, he asked the merchant to open a hanging box to take silver as payment.
He untied several bundles one after another, but there were no small pieces among them; instead, he took one as large as a thumb-top to pay him.

After the merchant had gone less than ten paces, the blind man asked the boy, "In my entire life of calculating fortunes, I have never obtained such a large piece of silver. How much silver is there in this man's box?"
"Is it silver? The youth replied, "I have opened several bundles; they are all solid ingots. There is indeed a great deal of this silver.
The blind man then cried out to the merchant, "Come here, come here! My reading of bone-marks is like that of a god. Let me examine you once more.

When the merchant returned to the pavilion, the blind man immediately began feeling his entire body, exclaiming in admiration at every turn. Gradually he felt his way up to the throat and neck, and suddenly—
With both hands tightly clasped, he clung to it until his life was extinguished. The merchant immediately lost consciousness; the boy and he then dragged and threw him into the midst of a wild grave.
Just as they were about to seize the chest and depart, a troop of soldiers suddenly dismounted and entered the pavilion to drink water.
One soldier, noticing tracks on the grassy path, hurried forward to investigate and saw a corpse with flames all over its body.
He was overcome with heat. He cried out in a loud voice, "In this desolate place, there is no one else! Surely these two blind men have conspired to kill me!
He then drew his sword and threatened the boy, saying, "Why did you plot to take their wealth and end their lives?
The boy, trembling with fear, pointed at the blind men and said, "It was they who harmed him; it was not I. The soldiers then hacked the blind men to pieces, cutting them down on the spot.
The flesh paste was taken away from the box. The young attendant was pressed down and brought to the prefecture, where he also collapsed and died.
The old man sighed and said, "Astrology is not an art for killing people. This blind man originally had no intention to kill.
Yet, upon hearing of much gold, the impulse to kill was suddenly stirred. Once the impulse to kill is stirred, one's own life is immediately extinguished. Thus one may know the nature of human life."
The world is born through goodness and dies through evil; birth and death depend upon the pivot (*ji*). Zhouzi said: "Sincerity is non-action;
the pivot is good or evil. That the pivot is so fearsome reaches this extreme—how can one not be cautious?
My Dharma heir, Jiuping Pengzi, while residing at Puhu, personally witnessed this and recounted it when he came to Yunju.
Wu Dao’ao, a woman of the Wu clan from Jining, sat in meditation and passed away amidst miraculous manifestations while devotedly reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
She had followed her husband, Tang, to Songjiang. Initially, she was extremely fierce and violent by nature, yet she alone among them was fond of the Buddha.
At the age of forty-three, she took refuge with Chan Master Bingkai and thereafter maintained a lifelong vegetarian fast, reciting the *Vajra* [Sūtra] day and night.

He had not emerged from his small tower for six years while studying the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Upon reaching the forty-ninth year, he suddenly told people, "I shall depart on such-and-such a day.
He said, "The Sūtra speaks of the indestructible body of the Vajra. After my departure, you may preserve this body for three years;

if it truly does not decay, only then will the Sūtra be proven efficacious. He then spoke a verse: "The wind sweeps away the clouds and mist, And the bright moon shines in perfect orb. [Realization is] complete..."
Yet he was without obstruction; within the pond, a golden lotus appeared. He then ordered his hair to be shaved, sat cross-legged, and passed away.

After three years had passed, the coffin was opened, and indeed his body remained incorruptible; the hair on his crown had grown half an inch long. Governor Liang then lacquered the body and built a hermitage to enshrine it, with a plaque inscribed "Seated Transformation.
It is currently located beside the local government school. Master Huaisu personally witnessed this event and composed a poem to commemorate it.

The poem says: He recited the Golden Sūtra with fierce diligence for six springs; His mind, like iron and stone, eventually attained realization. Even kings and dukes could not purchase such pure and adamantine bone;
Throughout his life, he left behind an indestructible body within his chamber. Sitting upright, he returned to the West through the power of meditative concentration;

On his departure, he spoke a gāthā to ferry the lost across the ford. Within the stūpa, the hair upon his crown was found startlingly long; It puts to shame those who, like myself, remain drunk in their dreams.
The Fang family, through sincere devotion and ritual recitation, had their entire household returned safely;
the Fang family of Tongcheng, having incurred punishment for an offense, reached Ningguo Tower and the whole clan, with utmost earnestness, took refuge in the Buddha and the heavens.
In the morning, he would hold the *jiaozhun* and recite the *Vajra* mantra; in the evening, he would prostrate before the Mother of the Stars (*Douxu*) to pray for his safe return.

One night, while he was prostrating before the stars, the lamp had already gone out. As he rose from his prostrations, the lamp suddenly lit itself again. On another deep night, a strange fragrance suddenly filled the room.
The master hurriedly called out, and the entire family knelt and offered prayers, saying: "We all look forward to his safe return. If we are granted this..."
Man-yuan requested the incense once more. As soon as he had finished speaking, a wondrous fragrance issued forth again; he offered his vows three times and received the response three times.
He was subsequently granted release by imperial grace and was indeed able to return home alive.
The Retired Elder said: "I and my elder brother Fangyu have long been known as inseparable friends. In the year of Gui-mao, while in Huangzhou, he dictated this account;
now, in Xin-hai, we have met again by the lake. He has requested that I record these events for inclusion in his collection.
That the sincerity of our family has produced such a response is manifest and undeniable."
My friend Xu Ziju, whose courtesy name is Ziwèi, is registered in Jiading County.

In the year of Gui-mao, while we were together in Huangzhou, he said to me: "When I previously examined the characters of my given name, I found that they correspond to the 'Middle' rank in the high-level civil service examinations."

"My younger brother was, in a previous life, a monk who collected discarded papers at a temple in the heavenly realm. When I asked for proof, he said, "In a dream within the palace examination halls, my body was that of a monk.
Before my quarters stood a wicker basket and a bamboo clip. Beside me I saw my friend from my hometown, Wu Jingguang, whose style name is Shunzheng;
he too wore monastic robes and carried a bag of rotten meat slung over his shoulder. He himself claimed that in a previous life he had been at such-and-such a temple."
He struck the mold and offered it to the assembly. Upon unrolling it, there were two lines of characters inside which read:
"Wu [Name] owes Xu [Name] one *shí* three *dǔ* of rice and one thousand *liǎng* of silver. Later, after he was registered in the *xiánshū*, both matters were verified:
his name appeared on the *gēngxū* examination list; he was sixth among the provincial leaders (*huìkuí*).
The retired elder said, "That gentleman practiced austerities to provide for the assembly; as a karmic reward, he attained the station of a wealthy and noble son.

He held the sacred teachings in high esteem, and though his family was poor, his talent and reputation were preeminent in the world. Having passed the imperial examinations at an advanced age, the Creator’s dispensation of retribution is unfailing in such a manner."
Throughout his life, Lord Wang of the Song dynasty collected discarded paper; he would wash it with fragrant water, burn it, and bury its ashes.
He fathered a son, Wang Zeng, who passed the three *yuan* (triple honors) examinations. See the "Essay on Reverencing Discarded Paper" by Wen Chang;
whether monk or layperson, follow this practice, for it will surely not fail to benefit you.
Dong Qi profited from using false scales, causing his family fortune to waste away in secret.
He was a Daoist priest at the Yuxiao Palace in Yuhang County. Every day he recited the *Duren Jing* (Scripture on Saving Humanity) before a dragon pool.
Suddenly, a dragon spirit manifested its form and said, "Master, your recitation of the scripture is most wonderful; however, it leaves my entire household restless, whether sitting or standing."

"Please come to the hall and recite [the scriptures]; I shall provide two jin of milk for your daily sustenance. From then on, he made offerings for ten years. Suddenly, for several days, no offerings were provided.
The Daoist continued as before to recite the sutras facing the pond. The dragon deity appeared once more, and the Daoist asked:
"Why have you not provided milk recently? The dragon deity replied, "This milk was originally not available within my palace.
A commoner named Dong Qi used a scale weighing fourteen *liang* to sell milk, and I would take the surplus to offer as sustenance for the Master.
Several days ago, Dong Qi died; now his father manages the shop and uses a scale calibrated at sixteen *liang*. I [cannot obtain it]."
He could not pull it out again, and therefore did not come to make an offering. It was not that he dared to breach his word of honor. The Daoist was deeply moved and sighed.
The old man said, "Nowadays, those in the marketplace all know how to use large scales and small measures, bending their hearts to take profit;
they consider themselves clever in their schemes. Yet when they are consumed by the skeletal deities in the darkness, no one knows of it. This is the end of clarity."
This matter appears in the *Yuhang County Gazette*. It is appended here as a "Wake-up Call for the World.
After the passing of the Venerable Master Feiyin, his cremation revealed many śarīra relics.
The Venerable Master Feiyin was a Dharma successor of the Elder Master Mi of Tiantong. He successively presided over Jin-sul, Tiantong, and Jingshan monasteries.
He governed the great monastery with strict discipline and correct commands, renowned throughout the realm as a master craftsman of the Great Vehicle.

In his later years, he resided at Fuyan on Shimen Mountain, where he presided over the assembly with diligent austerity and applied himself with precision and rigor to meditation and recitation. Later, when approaching the end of his life, he entrusted all matters, both great and small, to his successors with complete ease and detachment.
Having finished his final instructions, he sat upright and passed away. During the cremation, his cranial bone and teeth remained unburnt.

Relics were produced throughout his entire body, numbering nearly a thousand; the larger ones were as big as large beans. Later arrivals at the cremation site continued to receive them through their earnest entreaties, the number being beyond count.
Stupas were erected for him at Mount Huangbo in Min, as well as at Jin-su, Xing-yang, and other locations.
The retired elder said, "I saw fourteen of them at the place of Master Duguān while I was in Hankou.
Later, upon arriving at the place of Master Shixian in Nan'an, I again saw fifteen of them. Furthermore, at the home of Li the Axe-Man in Nanxiong, I saw six of them.
When floated on water, they all moved across the surface and merged into one; this was because they were all..."
The strength of a master’s Way lies in the certainty with which they bring about realization.
Chan Master Yuanzhi of Caoxi attained awakening through diligent cultivation and manifested auspicious signs at the end of his life.
Master Yuanzhi’s name was Quanfu; he was a Dharma heir of the late Elder Lingyan Ji and appeared in the world at Jiufeng in Chu.
Having succeeded to Huilin at Huayao and Nanyue at Fuyan, he later resided at Caoxi for one year before traveling west to Guangdong to propagate the Dharma.
Upon returning, he settled at Deshan. When the time came for his passing, he commanded that a basin of water and a blade be brought; he cast the blade into the water and sat upright, passing away.
During the cremation, a golden image of the Buddha appeared amidst the flames, causing both monastics and laypeople to rejoice in unison.
He was called a reincarnation of Zhou Jingang.
Ba’eng said, "Although Brother Yuanzhi presides over the school of the patriarchs, he has diligently practiced recitation day and night and observes the practice of eating only one meal at midday;
he is truly the one among my brothers who possesses the most virtuous conduct. His leadership was preeminent even as he approached his end amidst the flames."
A manifestation! Who would say that the practice of cultivation lacks spiritual efficacy?
The Venerable Tianbai, through his recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra*, finally heard celestial music.
Tianbai’s secular name was Xingchun. After receiving the precepts from Yunju, he abstained from food after noon and practiced day and night while residing there.
At Fucheng Hermitage in Yanfang, the master and his disciples would daily wait for traveling monks (*caryā-śramaṇas*) to welcome them back and provide them with offerings according to the Dharma.
Subsequently, they would recite the *Lotus Sūtra* together; one scroll was recited every day, and this practice was never neglected even while on the road. This continued for several years.

Later, as the master approached the end of his life, both the members of his household and the visiting monks heard celestial music resounding through the air. His disciple Xinjing came forward and addressed him, saying: "Master..."
He said, "My lifelong practice of true cultivation cannot be transmitted; otherwise, it would become mere falsehood. He then sat upright and passed away.
Upon cremation, a single bowl of *sāra* (solid essence—where the word *śarīra*, "relic," is likely omitted) was obtained.
Ba’eng said, “This was my head-disciple from the Yunju ordination platform. His practice was most authentic;
therefore, at the end, his radiance was greatly manifested in a most extraordinary manner. His stupa is now beside this hermitage, and I have composed an inscription for it.”
The novice, because his payment for the roster had not yet been completed, was shown by Weitian to be a former disciple under the late Master Fei of Fuyan;
at the time he received the precepts, he owed five mace and four cash on the roster.
Four years passed without his return. After the Elder had passed away, the Precept Disciple dreamed that Vajrapāṇi commanded him to return this silver, saying:
"Although it was originally five coins, by calculation according to its value, it amounts to two taels. The Precept Disciple said: "The Master has already entered nirvana;
to whom shall I return it? Vajrapāṇi replied: "The Master has passed on; you may deliver it to Lingyin Temple to complete this public affair."
According to the records: After Sengjue, he personally went to Lingyin Temple with the silver to recount the full circumstances. He offered it as a memorial to the late Elder.

The Elder struck the drum to address the assembly, instructing them to be cautious regarding cause and effect, saying: "The expenditures and receipts for the construction funds here are very extensive;
therefore, the Heavenly Lord Wei has manifested this to provide instruction and admonition."
The retired elder said, "This was an event from the year of Bingwu. When Master Lingjie first recounted it, I inquired about it, and the consensus of the assembly was the same.
Because Wang Pu had performed acts of goodness in his previous lives, he ultimately escaped the registers of the ghosts."
Wang Tao of Kunshan, courtesy name Yanfu, was selected as a *xiaolian* in the year Wumwu. He served as the Prefect of Suizhou.

When rebel bandits arrived in great numbers, he judged that the situation could not be sustained; he thus died in defense of his post within the prefectural hall. A single servant who had accompanied him escaped across the city walls to seek refuge.

Fearing that the great army would pass by during the night, he hid himself among the chaotic corpses beneath the city wall. At midnight, he suddenly saw a judge in crimson robes accompanied by several ghostly officials arrive with a lantern.
They began to examine the dead bodies, calling out each name one by one as they recorded them in the registers.

When the ghostly official reported Pu’s name to the King, the judge said, "This man accumulated merit in his previous life; his allotted span of life is not yet exhausted. He shall still be permitted to return to his home village. Why?
"Did she also die here? [The ghost] replied, "In the end, her name was not entered into the registers; the ghost-officials departed, and I ran back.

Because of poverty and illness, I could not immediately reach Kunshan. Her wife remained at home; initially she had vowed to remain steadfast, but later, as news was cut off, her relatives urged her to remarry.
When the crowd arrived at the door, she had already ascended the sedan chair. Just then, I suddenly arrived; we were startled and dispersed, and went out to welcome the assembly."
He was subsequently restored to his former health.
The retired elder said, "Master Yanfu is my fellow calligrapher and is like a thousand fathers to me.
When I returned home and recounted the matter of the ghost judge’s roll call, those who heard it were struck with such awe that their hair stood on end.
Yunxiu, because of his malicious nature, drove away his wife and ultimately suffered the retribution of becoming a snake.
Yunxiu, a monk of Chaoyin Hermitage in Taichang, was a disciple of the Dharma Master Sanji Gu. While living as a layman, his character was wicked.
He was fond of beating his wife. As she was dying, she made a vow, saying, "When I die, I will surely become a snake to take revenge upon you.
Yunxiu once mentioned this to others, saying, "Now that I have been a monk for many years and am far removed from my hometown, our grievance must surely be resolved.
One night, the Dharma Master felt a snake with his hand; he called out to the assembly to drive it away, telling them not to harm it, as his own bed happened to be right next to [the snake].
After the Master had left alone, at the following midnight the lamps were still burning. Huanxu suddenly cried out, "A snake has come!
The assembly pushed open the door to look, and it was already dead.
The retired elder said, "I know for myself that there is a karmic grievance; only through the practice of cultivation and the performance of memorial rites can such a grievance be resolved.

You, Yunxiu, merely thought that because the distance was great and the time long, you could escape the grievance by luck. But once the retribution of karma arrives, how can it be too late to bite your own heels?"
The young master Cai Fanglai, style name Jieming, was the younger son of Mr.
Yunyi, whose courtesy name was Mao-de, the late Minister Cai Zhongxiang of Kunshan.
In the year of Yisi, while traveling at Lingyin, he saw that the site was secluded and magnificent; there, within the hall of the monastery guardian deity (galan), he made a vow.
He asked, "When shall I be able to leave home to become a monk and practice here on this ground? Upon returning home, he suddenly fell ill.

He saw the various *kṣetrapāla* deities of the monastery before him, who told him: "Since you desire to leave home, you have already found a family of the Tang surname living before the mountains of India."
"He is quite fond of the good. You should take rebirth as his son; once you have reached the age of eighteen, you may leave the household life to become a monk.
Having finished speaking, he took the soul upon his back and departed. The family members surrounded him, weeping and clinging to him in an attempt to detain him.

Caijun said to the family, "You may go to Lingyin Temple to seek the divination of the Great Monk of Complete Virtue. If the temple deity grants permission, I shall be able to keep you here by force."

His wife, surnamed [Name], galloped to the mountain like a shooting star. She informed the deceased elder of the circumstances and led the assembly to present offerings, recite mantras, and entreat the monastery guardian deity with lamentation.
After about three divinations, the wife returned, and Cai Jun was subsequently restored to life.
The retired elder said: "In the spring of the Wushen year, Cai Jun’s wife came personally to Lingyin Temple to present the *Record of Resuscitation* written by her husband.
The details of its beginning and end were extremely thorough.
A monk from north of the Yangtze River, who had been bound by attachment to his worldly possessions, was able to achieve liberation through this meritorious dedication."

There was a monk in Taizhou named [Name]. He had served the late Master Sanmei for many years and served as the head of the administrative quarters (Jianyuan) of the Dizang Hall at a certain location.
By nature he was quite stingy, never spending a single coin frivolously.

After his passing, whenever the night grew deep and quiet, two monks staying in the hall would frequently see the head of the quarters manifesting his form. At first, he would straighten the shoes of the two monks; his face appeared...
Filled with grief and suffering, he next ascended to the Buddha’s seat and reached out his hand to touch the *Dizang* flower crown.

Thereafter, he departed with a playful laugh. The assembly informed the Elder who had been there first. The Elder said, "This karmic obstruction must surely have left something behind within the flower crown;

that is why he remains bound by attachment and refuses to let it go. He ordered the ladder to be raised and someone to search inside. Indeed, eighty pieces of silver were found. Immediately, he commanded that a vegetarian feast be prepared.
When the memorial service for the posthumous offerings was concluded, he never appeared again from that time forth.
Baiweng said, "The late Master often spoke of this to me directly:
Wang Yangquan had attained rebirth in the Pure Land by changing his occupation and practicing cultivation."
Wang Yangquan, a citizen of Hangzhou, initially served as the head of a sheep-slaughterers' guild and slaughtered countless animals. Later, while ill, he beheld a flock of sheep seeking their lives;
struck with fear, he completely changed his occupation, observing the long fast and serving the Buddha. He personally recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* three thousand times.
In his later years, inspired by a Zen master, he further performed prostrations to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* day and night. At the age of eighty...
Eleventh: Previously, when he saw an official messenger arrive to summon him, he raised his voice in defiance and refused, saying, "I shall wait for the Buddha to come before I go.

Five days later, as expected, he beheld the Great-Body Buddha appear, extending his hand to welcome and guide him; thereupon, he passed away with a serene countenance. All who saw or heard of this were moved to deep admiration and sighs of wonder.
The Retired Elder said, "This is what is called 'rebirth while carrying one's karma.

Yet, Zhang Shanhe achieved this through merely ten recitations at the moment of death, whereas this [case] involved cultivation accumulated over several decades. Even with heavy karma, it is like a many-year-old dark room being pierced by the brilliant sun.
Among those who create worldly karma, everyone is like a house next door; who else is able to act as you have?"
To sever and reform one’s errors is indeed the courageous practice of cultivation. That such an example exists is sufficient proof that the Buddha’s words are not false.
Spoken by Master Jixian in the fifth month of the Gengxu year.
A fishing boat used a clever ruse to drown a man and immediately reported it as a self-inflicted death.
At the Zhajiang-Jingkou ferry crossing, a merchant from Wuhu was traveling on a fishing boat when he saw a giant fish in their net.

He opened his trunk, selected some silver, and purchased the fish’s release. Unbeknownst to him, there were whole silver ingots among the coins, which he inadvertently revealed. The old fisherman then devised a scheme to entice the merchant.
He said, "If we wish to release these fish, we must go to a place where there are no nets on boats. Thus, he set sail northward toward a desolate region.
There, they cast a large net over the merchants and hurled them into the river. The net drifted downstream with the current, rising and sinking amidst the waves until it reached a calm anchorage.
There, the soldiers suddenly saw a great fish leap from the air and, competing with one another, [struck it].
They came upon a fishing net; upon untying it, they found it was a person who had not yet lost consciousness.
He explained his situation to the soldiers, who immediately seized the fisherman and brought him to the General’s residence, where he was executed. The silver was returned to the merchant.
Master Ba’eng said, “This is precisely what occurred in the second month of the Gengxu year. Shi Yi and Master Heyan came from Zhenjiang;
they saw it with their own eyes and spoke of it themselves.”
The scholar Shen from North of the River suffered severe retribution for defacing the *Platform Sūtra*.
This Mr. Shen had been enrolled in the state schools since his youth; relying on his talent, he acted recklessly.

While reading in a secluded temple, he saw the *Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch* and wantonly used a vermilion brush to deface it. Upon returning home, he died suddenly. He appeared in a dream to his father and said, "Tell him that because he..."
The *Platform Sūtra* was currently in hell; his body was bound with flaming shackles, and the suffering was unbearable.

His father went to the temple where he had studied to search for the *Platform Sūtra*, hoping to wash away the traces of ink so that he might escape from his torment. The father’s grief was beyond measure.

He entered the temple to search for it and indeed found the original manuscript. He immediately washed away the old markings and, with a resolute mind, commissioned a new carving of one copy to circulate, so as to repent for his son’s transgressions.
The Retired Elder said, "The Great Master Sixth Patriarch manifested as a great being in human form at Caoxi.
The *Platform Sūtra* he taught is no different from the Golden Sūtra. How reckless was Shen’s defacement! I am fortunate that you, Father, have re-engraved and printed it for circulation;

not only will this liberate us from suffering, but it will surely cause us to transcend this life and be reborn in a good realm. As the ancients said: "One falls because of the ground one stands upon."

He rose from the ground once more; was this not so? Several Chan practitioners who saw the newly carved edition told me that because his friend had mistakenly caused the death of a person, his register of merit and longevity was suddenly depleted.
This friend, Zhi [Name], had long been renowned for his talent. In the summer of the Jihou year, he went to the examination in Jiaxing. During the day...
He saw a ghost enter his belly; he then collapsed to the ground and, uttering a Northern dialect, cried out for his life. His servant hurriedly prepared a boat to carry him back.
He invited Master Xilian, the abbot of Youlan Temple, to inquire, saying, "From what direction have you come, you malevolent ghost?
How dare you harass Lord Zhixiang? The ghost replied in a loud voice, "I am no malevolent ghost. It is because of a karmic connection from a former enmity that..."
He arrived and came to demand retribution. Master Lian interrogated him regarding the cause. The ghost said, "At the beginning of the Ming dynasty, I served as a deputy general under Xu Zhongshan;
my surname was Hong and my given name was Zhu. My commanding officer, General Yao, saw that my wife, Lady Wang, possessed a beautiful countenance."
Possessing greed and malice, Yao instigated a rebellion by bandits in a certain region. He ordered me, with seven hundred soldiers who were mostly old and weak, to campaign against them.
My strength was insufficient; my army was utterly defeated. Yao captured my wife, who hanged herself to death.
I harbored this deep-seated enmity and plotted for generations to take revenge. However, in his final days, Lord Yao regretted his ways and practiced cultivation. Consequently, he was reborn as Gao.
In his third generation, he was again a monk of virtuous conduct; in the fourth, he was a great wealthy man who delighted in charity.
I have been unable to repay his kindness in any of these instances. Now, in the fifth generation, during the years of You and Xu, there shall be successive victories.

However, in a certain year, because he manipulated the brush and ink to cause injury to four tea-sellers in Yuhang County, the Underworld has already struck his name from the registers of official emolument. Therefore—
"I have come here specifically to claim my life. Hearing these words, Master Xilian found them well-ordered and proceeded to instruct him, saying:

"Your words are precise; they are certainly not false. However, within our Buddhist teachings there are sublime sutras and repentance rites that can resolve your grievances and untie your karmic knots, enabling you to transcend this life and be reborn in the blissful realm of the Sugata.
Why suffer by seeking only retribution to satisfy a momentary fit of anger?"
The ghost said in alarm, "If it is truly so, that would be most excellent. However, I fear it may be false and not real.

If you indeed establish a *dōjō*, I shall immediately leave Master Zhi and go to the central hall to pay homage to the Buddha. Thereupon, Master Xilian was requested to draw up a contract and burn it;
thus, the Dharma assembly was established. Master Zhi suddenly awoke, but several days later he fell to the ground again and lost consciousness.

The voice from the north replied: "I have already been delivered to a higher rebirth; why have you come back? The Master Xilian then reprimanded him, saying, "You were sent away for the sake of your posthumous advancement.
For what reason have you returned? The ghost said, "By the power of the Buddha, I have indeed attained a superior rebirth and shall certainly not return.
Those who have now come to claim my life are four tea-sellers; it is not I. Fearing that you, Master, might suspect me of lacking sincerity, I have come to inform you."
"Listen. Having finished speaking, he departed. Subsequently, Master Zhi fell ill; before two nights had passed, he died suddenly. Ba’eng said:
"In the autumn of the辛亥 year, I carried my alms bowl to Jiashan and stayed at Youlan Temple for over twenty days.
Master Xilian recounted this to me in great detail. This principle of cause and effect is most certain; it is known by every household and understood by all."
Therefore, these have been arranged in sequence and appended here; their names are concealed while their manifest fruits are recorded.
